en: The Scripture of the Great Brahma Heavenly King Asking the Buddha to Resolve Doubts:
Chapter One: The Preface Chapter Two: The Chapter on Plucking the Flower Chapter Three:
The Chapter on the Lunar Disk Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Dharma Realm
The Scripture of the Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve His Doubts Chapter Five: The Six Great Elements Chapter Six: Subduing Māra Chapter Seven:
Rebirth in the Pure Land *Mahābrahmādeva-rāja-prcchā-buddha-saṃśaya-vinodana-sūtra*
Chapter One: The Introduction.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa together with a great assembly of eighty thousand bhikṣus, including the Venerable [Ānanda], the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
He was the foremost leader, accompanied by an assembly of eighty thousand bodhisattvas, with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Ajita Bodhisattva,
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva of Vows and Conduct, and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as their leaders. He was also joined by the great Brahma kings,
Śakra Devānām Indra, Vaiśravaṇa King, Mahādhararāja King, and immeasurable hosts of devas, as well as the sea dragons.
The King, the Yakṣa Kings, the Asura Kings, and immeasurable hosts of deities were present; King Ajātaśatru, King Prasenajit, ministers, Brahmins, and immeasurable multitudes of people were present;
and the Daḍha hell-beings, the Yama-mouthed hungry ghosts, the golden lion, the six-tusked elephant king, and immeasurable non-human beings were present.
Each of them prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One descended from the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and, surrounded by the great assembly, flew toward the east for hundreds of thousands of *li*. There was a land named Great Seven-Jeweled China;
in the center of that country was a high mountain called the Five-Jewel Terrace, where Mañjuśrī constantly preached the Dharma. Upon reaching this mountain, he addressed the great assembly.
It is said: Formerly, in this land, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifested as the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna Heaven in order to transform the human realm.

Having vanished from his Brahmā palace, he descended to be born in a royal palace. Assuming the body of a great-virtue dragon, he expounded the principles of heaven and the laws of the five phases (*wuxing*) and the transformations of the vital breaths (*qi*) that produce good fortune and calamity.
When the earth submerged and returned to the heavens, he became the Lord of Spring. Thus did Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifest himself.
The two Great Brahma Kings of the First Dhyāna, for the sake of transforming the human realm, vanished from their celestial palaces and descended into royal palaces as Fire-Virtue Ox-Head.

They expounded upon the benefits of the earth, various medicinal herbs, and the treatment of poisons to assist the vital energies of humanity; when the earth dissolved, they returned to heaven to serve as the lords of the summer season.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifested as Śakra, and for the sake of transforming the human realm, vanished from his celestial palace and descended [to be born].
The royal palace is the embodiment of the virtue of earth (*pṛthivī-guṇa*). It teaches the Great Way of the Dharma of the human mind and the five relations of human ethics.

When the earth subsides, it returns to heaven, acting as the sovereign of the earthly realm. These three kings constitute the powerful Three Powers (*trikaṭaka*). They expound the virtuous nature of humanity;

relying on conventional teachings, they reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). All of this is due to the compassionate transformation and manifestation of Avalokiteśvara; thus, in this land, there is Avalokiteśvara.

"There is a connection. In the age of the Final Dharma, my teaching shall circulate; while the conditions for other Buddhas have ceased, only Avalokiteśvara remains to bring benefit through transformation throughout all eternity.
Having spoken these words, the three kings appeared, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is as the Buddha has now said."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and, for the sake of the three kings and the great assembly, also traveled eastward for ten thousand *li* across the sea.
Within the sea there was a country named Mahādivākara; to the east, west, south, and north within the sea were other countries which were its tributary states.
When the World-Honored One reached the seashore of this country, he addressed the great assembly, saying: "In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, [he] observed..."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara transformed himself into the tenth Brahmā King of the Form Realm and addressed the first Brahmā King:

"Descend into the void of space, to the celestial realms of the Desire Realm, and further down to the created lands. The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara transformed the first Brahmā King to serve as the Great Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna.
He commanded the King and his consort to provide offerings below, within the void of space, and to successively create the worlds beneath. They proceeded to create them.
The Great Earth finally created this land, along with its surrounding seas, central mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees.
There was a celestial maiden named Subhāṣitārthā (妙辨財), who, having served as a great field of merit in the form of a woman for immeasurable kalpas, came as the king’s daughter;
she then became the Sun Disk and the Moon Disk, presiding over the four continents and her retinue.
They belong to the Immeasurable One and dwell within this land, acting either as leaders or as companions. Therefore, in this land, Avalokiteśvara has a karmic affinity with beings.

During the age of the Final Dharma, when my teachings are disseminated, the affinities for other Buddhas will have ceased, and only Avalokiteśvara shall remain to bring benefit through his transformations throughout all eternity.
Having spoken these words, a goddess appeared, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, just as the Buddha now..."
Having spoken thus, at that time the World-Honored One rose from his seat and, together with the goddesses and the great assembly, proceeded toward the east.
Within that ocean there were various lands; the sentient beings of these lands were by nature close to the state of animals, even though they dwelt within my True Dharma.
It gradually spread, yet it was difficult for anyone to realize and enter into; it served merely to establish karmic connections as the conditions for attaining Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned with the great assembly to his original location at the summit of Vulture Peak, where he arranged his seat and sat down.
He addressed the great assembly: "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa. If there is any among you who wishes to inquire about the Dharma, ask freely.
At that time, the great assembly sat in silence; there was not a single sound from anyone.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not manifest supernatural powers, yet revealed wondrous marks.
He accomplished the Lotus of the Tathatā of the Great Vaipulya Buddha-Mind; he accomplished the Dharma-body enjoyed since five hundred *kalpas* past;

he accomplished the Buddhas’ ability to exhaustively realize the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; and he accomplished the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Āgama*, the *Vaipulya*, the *Prajñā*, and the Single Reality.
The Buddha Prabhūtaratna has accomplished the wondrous Dharma of the Lotus Sutra and testified to the *tathatā* (suchness) of his great vow.

He has accomplished the state of having entered extinction yet not being extinguished since immeasurable kalpas past; he has accomplished the jeweled stupa, which is the stupa of the *dharmadhātu* and the land of eternal quiescent light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*).

He has accomplished the sharing of his seat, which is the very embodiment of the *dharmakāya* of both self and other through the union of principle and wisdom. Thus, he has accomplished these two personages, the World-Honored Ones.

The Tathāgata Niyu (Nirvāṇa) resides upon his seat on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Flower-Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍaka-lokadhātu*), while the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has already returned to the Jewel-Attained Quiescent Light World (*Ratnasaṃbhava-prabhāsaviśuddha-lokadhātu*);
these two lands are interfused, achieving a single land. This is precisely what is opened and revealed within the minds of ordinary beings.

Originally possessing the Buddha-mind, ordinary beings attain Buddhahood through the Great and Sublime Dharma. This is precisely why he intended to entrust this treasury of the sublime Dharma to his successor, Mahākāśyapa;
such was the underlying reason. At that time, the World-Honored One did not rise from the Dharma seat of the wondrous path of the Lotus Sutra.
Chapter Two: Plucking the Flower.

At that time, the Great Brahma King, Lord of the Sahā World, named Fangguang (Vipula), took a *mahā-brahma-flower* of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which was the root of the accomplishment of the trichiliocosm, and offered it to the Buddha, then withdrew.

Having prostrated, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, since the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment fifty years ago, you have expounded various teachings and provided various instructions to transform and deliver all classes of sentient beings according to their capacities. Yet, there remains a supreme Great Dharma that has not yet been taught;
for my sake and for those who practice the Bodhisattva path in the final age—ordinary beings who wish to cultivate the Way of the Buddha—"
He expounded and proclaimed this extensively. Having spoken these words, he relinquished his body to become a seat, adorned with celestial garments, and caused the Tathāgata to sit upon it.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat upon this precious throne and accepted this lotus; without speaking or uttering a word, he merely held the lotus flower.
Upon entering the great assembly, the gathering of eighty-four thousand people and devas all became silent.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, seeing the Buddha’s act of holding up a flower to show the multitude, was suddenly enlightened and broke into a broad smile.
The Buddha then declared, "It is so! I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the reality-limit (dharmatā) which is without..."

This is the Dharma-gate of subtle marks. It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings. As a total retention that sustains all, it enables ordinary beings to attain Buddhahood.
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is now being entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Having spoken thus, he remained silent.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One, this wondrous..."
Ah! I recall events from immeasurable kalpas in the past. At the site where the Buddha Dīpaṃkara preached the Dharma, I resolved my mind upon Bodhi and followed the Buddha in his practice.
Furthermore, at the place where the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, it was within that teaching that I attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna).
Having become an arhat, they further hear the teaching on the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and enter the bodhisattva path.
Without wavering from their previous fruit, they accomplish the Mahāyāna path and draw near to the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). From where does such wondrous wisdom originate?
All [beings] have come from the mind of the ordinary person since time immemorial. That mind of time immemorial is equal to the mind of all Buddhas;

this is the Dharma-body, and this is called attaining Buddhahood. To perceive this mind is not to be found within verbal teachings, rational instructions, intellectual understanding, or the interpretation of words and characters.
However, within the manifestation of the mind, one does not rely on *samādhi* nor expect the attainment of fruits.
When causes and conditions ripen, even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) immediately perceive this; therefore, the Buddha-way is transmitted among ordinary people without interruption.

If this Dharma did not exist, there would only be noble ones (*ārya*) who attain the Way through the attainment of fruits, and there would be no ordinary *bhikṣus*, *bhikṣuṇīs*, *upāsakas*, or *upāsikās*.

Regarding those who attain the Buddha-way: if, within the turbid and evil world of the Final Dharma, there were not even one person among thousands or tens of thousands who realizes the fruit—because no such realization exists—the transmission of the Buddha-way would be severed, and only its name would remain, with no sign of the Way.
Because this Dharma exists, the signs of the Buddha-way are transmitted; it shall not be terminated in the final age. The Buddha said, "Excellent, Māra."
“Kāśyapa, it is as you have said. The manner in which the seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, transmitted the Dharma was like this;
the manner in which the disciples of those seven Buddhas transmitted the Dharma was likewise so. After my parinirvāṇa, I now entrust the great treasury of the Dharma to you.
You must be able to uphold, transmit, and propagate the True Dharma, following in the lineage of the Way of the Mind so that it shall never be severed.”
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from the Brahma King’s body-seat, which was a wondrously adorned celestial throne, and sat upon his original seat.
He addressed the Great Brahma King: "In the past, throughout immeasurable eons, you cultivated the Bodhisattva path and dwelt in the stage of high rank;
thus you are able to inquire about this Dharma. In the turbid and evil world of the final dharma, you shall cause the great path of the Buddhas' mind-dharma to continue uninterruptedly."
[All] severances are entirely due to relying upon your power. There is still that which remains to be contemplated;
you may ask about it all as you wish. The Tathāgata shall expound the True Dharma for you. The Great Brahmā King said: "Excellent, World-Honored One!
Grant me leave to ask such things. I shall now question you. Has the Tathāgata previously taught it in a sūtra? Has he not yet taught it? Has he already shown it? The Buddha—
He addressed the Great Brahma King, saying: "I have already spoken of this before; since I have spoken it, Śāriputra said that it cannot be expressed in words.
At that time, Śāriputra realized this Dharma face-to-face and immediately received the prediction of his future attainment as the Buddha Flower-Light (Puṣyarasmi).
Furthermore, the dragon girl offered a single precious jewel, which was beyond description.
The Dragon Girl took a precious jewel and offered it to the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata accepted the jewel immediately;
as soon as he received it, the Dragon Girl, by means of this path of the Buddha-mind, attained Buddhahood right then and there.
The Great Brahmā King said, "If this is so, then today the Tathāgata has made this single dharma the most authentic. The Buddha said:
It is so. It is as you have said. Śāriputra has not been apart from me since past kalpas, and it is likewise today.
Before long, I shall enter parinirvāṇa and leave nothing behind for my followers. The dragon girl has already attained Buddhahood in another land;
she is no longer my disciple, and her dharma shall not be transmitted—it is all as if she were deaf. Today there is only Mahā...

Kāśyapa, you shall transmit the true image of the Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the final dharma age, the five turbidities, and the latter five hundred years, it is only through you, Kāśyapa, that the Buddha-way shall not be severed;
it is entrusted to you alone for transmission. For this reason, it is called "the sole reality. The Great Brahmā King asked:
"The Tathāgata previously spoke of the 'latter five hundred years. What constitutes those five hundred years?"

"It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Regarding those five hundred years: after my parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma shall abide in the world for five thousand five hundred years—eight hundred years of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), one thousand two hundred years of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), and five thousand five hundred years of the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*).

The 'five hundred years' refers to all the years remaining after the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma have passed. The Great Brahmā King said, "The True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma..."
Regarding the "final dharma" and the "latter five hundred years," one might ask: in what world and in what country do these occur? The Buddha said:
"That world is the human world, not the world of devas nor the world of nāgas. Furthermore, that country is within Jambudvīpa."
It occurs in various countries, not necessarily in a single one. Why is this? The worlds of devas and nāgas are the worlds of the sages, and they have no fixed limit.
Only the world of humans has the upper realms being pure and the lower realms turbid, and the upper realms flourishing while the lower realms decline; therefore, it has a limit.
Furthermore, from country to country, times change and circumstances shift. In some places there is protection by devas, while in others there is protection by sages;

in some there is no protection by devas, and in others no protection by sages. In some there is protection by spirits, while in others there is protection by immortals; in some there is no protection by spirits, and in others no protection by immortals.

The capacities of sentient beings are immeasurable, and nations follow the capacities of their people; therefore, it is not necessarily the case that this applies to only one nation. The Brahma King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is so. It is as the Buddha has taught: the capacities of nations differ; some possess the conditions for connection, while others do not."
There are those who protect and bring peace, and there are those who protect against hardship; here they flourish while there they decline, and here they perish while there they thrive.
After the Dharma of the Buddha gradually spread to the East during the final five hundred years, the transmission of the Dharma was preserved without interruption, benefiting all sentient beings.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, since Your appearance in the world more than forty years ago, You have preached the Dharma in various ways.
How can there be a 'never-before-heard' Dharma? How can there be a Dharma that reaches beyond words?
We pray that for the sake of all people and devas in the world, You will be able to manifest it yourself. Having spoken thus, he held up a great golden thousand-petaled *bala* flower.
Having thus paid homage to the Buddha, he withdrew and offered his own body as a seat.

With sincere mindfulness and aspiration, the World-Honored One sat upon that seat and, with a radiant countenance, held up a flower. At that time, among the assembly of hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, [the Venerable Mahākāśyapa] smiled.
The bhikṣus were all silent. At that time, in the midst of the assembly, there was only the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who, upon seeing this manifestation, broke into a smile.
He rose from his seat, joined his palms, and stood upright, breathing but without speaking.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the true mark which is markless.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings. Whether one has wisdom or lacks wisdom, it is realized through the conditions of encounter.
Today, I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. Mahākāśyapa, in future ages you shall serve [it]."
"All Buddhas shall attain Buddhahood; today, you too are worthy to be teachers of the world. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa.
You bhikṣus should all rely upon Mahākāśyapa to enter the gateway of the Mahāyāna and cultivate the path of the Buddha.
He addressed Mahākāśyapa: "There is no other dharma; there is only the single nature of mind."
The Buddhas—the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, and the Buddhas of the future—have already taught, are now teaching, and will continue to teach only this.
All Buddhas, relying on the nature of the one mind, have already realized, are currently realizing, and will realize the Buddha-way.
It is the same for all sentient beings. If one were to claim that there are other dharmas, there would still be something further [to seek] beyond the Buddhas.

"Becoming a Buddha" and "sentient beings becoming Buddhas" are the doctrines of external paths; they are not the teachings of the Seven Buddhas, nor are they the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Kāśyapa, you should know that the eighty thousand treasuries of the canon which you have been entrusted with are the teachers of these various doctrines; they are the vehicles for the vessel of the one mind.
For example, just as there are ox-carts and horse-carts in the world, these are the vehicles of all dharmas for crossing over the path.
It is a vessel. All the sutras of the teaching are likewise so. You are able to receive and uphold them.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, this Dharma is truly difficult to encounter. It is indeed the direct path; it is indeed the wondrous path. In the past, I met the Buddha and left the household life."
In their practice, they were exclusively weary of birth and death, seeking only nirvana; they cultivated only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and did not seek this Dharma.

They merely understood the principle of emptiness and did not recognize this Dharma. Through many years of arduous effort and difficult ascetic practices, they attained the state of an Arhat—truly a difficult achievement to contemplate.
Today, the Tathāgata’s most supreme and wondrous instruction requires only a single *kṣaṇa*; it is neither a matter of years nor of kalpas, and is by no means difficult.

It is wonderfully easy. It causes me to attain Buddhahood without any doubt. Although it is not actually until the completion of kalpas that one attains the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the purple-golden hue, and the wondrous enlightenment of Buddhahood, one truly knows the Dharma-body;
this mind is the Buddha. All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess a single, wondrous body. Reflecting now upon the past, throughout many years, I have practiced difficult austerities.

"Austerities are laborious yet fruitless. Furthermore, for many years you have sought emptiness and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), but these are all merely provisional dharmas and not the true dharma.
Today you have realized this Dharma of True Emptiness: its appearance is precisely empty, yet its nature is not empty;
its essence is unconditioned, yet its nature is perfectly complete. All sentient beings rely solely upon this Dharma to attain Buddhahood. Thus the Buddha told [them].
Mahākāśyapa said, "So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said. In the future, you shall attain Buddhahood;
such is this Dharma, just as it is for me today. At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he rose from his seat and returned to sit upon his original seat.
He remained without speech and without movement, and the assembled multitude likewise became silent and still, all imbued with a sublime aura.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, excellent! World-Honored One, you have been able to explain this so well.
After the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, how shall sentient beings of future generations enter [the path]? How shall they practice?

I pray that you will grant me the essential and refined Dharma-methods for entering, attaining entry, and practicing. The Buddha told the Great Brahmā King: "King of Devas, listen attentively and reflect upon it well."

I shall explain this. The faculties and capacities of sentient beings are diverse and immeasurable: some enter through the principle, some through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), some through causes and conditions, and some through upholding and demonstrating [the teachings];
they are not uniform. Your Majesty possesses only faith, yet you are able to enter the most supreme path.
How could one give rise to faith without relying on the nature of the mind? Otherwise, one would not attain Buddhahood. Why is this so? Because within the mind...
Outside of one's own nature, there is no path to Buddhahood. One who understands this and seeks it with sincerity is a person capable of traversing this Way.

[Such a one may possess] wisdom like Śāriputra, extensive learning like Ānanda, eloquence like Pūrṇa, understanding of emptiness like Subhūti, observance of the precepts like Upāli, supernormal powers like Maudgalyāyana, and the divine eye like Aniruddha.

In this way, these individuals shall all fail to attain Buddhahood. Why is this? Because they have all attained the provisional function of the mind-nature (*cittatā*), but have not yet attained the true essence of the mind-nature.
To realize only the essential body of nature would necessarily extinguish the Buddha-way. Thus one should understand.
Those who seek with sincerity can enter this path. O Heavenly King, there may be those who know and perceive the wondrous, true substance of the nature of mind;

at the moment of such knowing and perceiving, they realize that wondrous principle. Without distraction and without separation, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, their mind and body are fused as one.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—their faculties and natures are fused into one. To practice in this way is to walk the Buddha-way.

Whether a lay bodhisattva or a monastic bodhisattva, there is no difference and no distinction; it is solely by means of this single path of fusion. At this very moment, I have already attained the Buddha-way;
thus, practicing within the mundane world or the supramundane world is without fault.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King asked Kāśyapa, "The World-Honored One has in the past taught various doctrines.
Regarding the principles of those teachings, what difference is there today in the mind you have received from the Buddha?
He said to the Brahmā King, "Virtuous one, do not ask such a thing. If there were any difference in the principles of the teachings previously spoken by the World-Honored One..."
Regarding the mind received this very day, those various teachings are merely false doctrines.
If there were a mind received this day by the Blessed One that differed from the principles of the teachings previously expounded, then that would indeed be "mind.
But this single principle of mind is such that there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference between it and all other teachings. If there is a practitioner who says:
The various doctrinal principles differ from this principle of mind; these are merely what is taught by non-Buddhists and celestial Māras.
Not only do they fail to understand the principles taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras, but they also do not understand my teaching on the single principle of mind.

If one were to know the principle of mind, one should know that the doctrinal principles are of one and the same principle without difference. As for those various doctrinal principles that appear to differ, it is because...

Although there may be benefit, it is not ultimate. This teaching of knowledge and vision is exclusively real and non-dual. Even if other teachings were to exist, their benefit would be merely partial;
this does not mean that others lack a degree of benefit. Their nature is taught as a single aspect, like the light of a star compared to the sun.
To analyze light into starlight is not to say that the stars have no light; so too, the minor points— the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
the Five Precepts and the Ten Wholesome Actions, the mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land,
the observance of the precepts and seated meditation, and the various great Bodhisattvas of expedient means— are all merely minor points within that [ultimate truth].
This teaching is like the light of the sun; other teachings are like the light of the stars.
Although the stars fill the sky, they are not called "day. When the sunlight appears, the night sky becomes day.
Though other teachings exist in the world, they are not called the Buddha-dharma; for it is the Buddhas who bring sentient beings to correctness.
The defiled land is the pure land; birth and death are themselves nirvana. The three periods of time are eternally one period;
the dharmas of the world are themselves the Buddha-dharma. Conditioned phenomena are truly unconditioned.
To know and see such teachings and their practitioners— this is called the existence of the Buddha-dharma, and it is also called the existence of my world.
When the Buddha spoke these words, there were hundreds of thousands of people in the assembly who all understood the unsurpassed path;
they were taught the principles of the nature of mind so as to awaken to them. Those who transmit the principle of the mind achieve the Way of the Buddha by transmitting it through the mind.
Having attained the principle of the nature of mind, those who teach the Way of the Buddha—whether entering the mind gradually or entering the mind suddenly—differ not in their speed.
It is the same. The principle is likewise identical. For example, a person from a land in the east points to the solar disk and says, "This solar disk goes from my eastern sky to that western sky.
A person from a land in the west also points to the solar disk and says, "This solar disk comes from that eastern sky to my western sky," and so forth.
Although they differ in their words regarding its coming and going from here or there, they do not err in identifying it as the sun; such is the case with the solar disk.
He said: "When one speaks of the principles of east and west in daily discourse, there is no discrepancy. The teachings of the Tathāgata are likewise:
whether transmitted through the oral teaching or the mind-to-mind transmission, the manifestations shown differ, yet the underlying principle is one and the same."
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Regarding this Way of the nature of vision, should only bhikṣus practice this Way? Or may those who dwell at home also universally practice it?

The Buddha said: "O Heavenly King, as for the Way of the nature of mind, both those who have left the home life and those who dwell at home, as well as devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits [may practice it]."

All are fully complete; how could they be limited to the bhikṣus alone? There are only the modes of conduct for the laity and those who have left the home life, which differ from one another and are not uniform. As for the conduct of those who have left the home life:

The parents have already been pardoned; one leaves the parents' home and takes over their duties. Because the Buddhas of the three periods have no sovereign lord, the Bodhisattva who takes over these duties establishes a household for the Buddha’s form.
This is like a Buddha in his physical body; it possesses the Buddha’s relics, being as if the Buddha were still in the world.

Because they have transcended the mundane world, they do not pay homage to kings, nor do they revere celestial beings or seers. They seek neither wealth nor treasures, but carry only a single alms bowl.
They do not store extra clothing, but maintain only the three robes. Dwelling peacefully in deep mountains, beneath trees, or in rocky caves, they purify their minds and cleanse their bodies.
With clear awareness of the body, one realizes oneself as the primordial Buddha; this is the single dharma-gate of the Buddha-body.
Chapter Three: The Moon Disk.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "Mahākāśyapa, what has been taught by the seven Buddhas does not differ in its path."

The Buddhas attain enlightenment through no other dharma than this single knowledge and vision: by clearly perceiving the nature and principle of the form of one's own single mind, one immediately becomes a Buddha.
If there were any other dharma that could cause one to become a Buddha, it would be the false dharma of Māra Pāpīyān, the Heavenly Demon.
Kāśyapa, you should know that beneath the Bodhi tree, I subdued Māra and attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, I saw the form of the mind completely and saw the principle of the mind completely. I perceived the essence of the mind as being in the shape of a lunar disc.

The Buddhas appeared and immediately conferred upon me the seal of certification, declaring that I would attain Buddhahood; for it was through my practice over immeasurable kalpas of the distant past that this was accomplished.
Although I do not manifest the attainment of Buddhahood now, even though I have not yet attained it, my Buddha-body is already perfected. I am now certified to this.
When a person immediately perceives their own body as being the original Buddha, this is known as "seeing the Buddha.
I now bestow a prediction upon this person that in a future life, before long, they shall achieve the fruition of a Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, just like Mahākāśyapa in this present assembly.

Although he has already realized and seen his own *dharmakāya*, because he has not yet fulfilled the six perfections over the course of kalpas, he has not yet attained the *dharmakāya* of the wondrous enlightenment of Buddhahood.

Nevertheless, because one knows and perceives that the self-nature is the body of the Buddha-dharma, and realizes that the Buddhas of the ten directions are of one essence and one person, one attains the seal of certification from the Buddhas.
Thus, one shall attain Buddhahood in the future before all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"O Heavenly King, it is like the lunar disc in the world. During the new moon, the first quarter, the full moon, and the waning moon, the moon does not appear.

Although it is indeed the lunar disc, people do not call it 'the moon. During the new moon, because the sun is near, people do not see it; though the common folk do not believe it exists, those who know recognize it as the moon.
It is like a person who has seen their true nature upon first generating the bodhicitta: the worldly do not know it, but the practitioner knows it. (3)
At twilight, the sky manifests three parts of light; although it has not yet formed a full orb, the world knows it is the moon.
So too, one who has realized their true nature can fully manifest their inherent virtue, and all people recognize this. Mahākāśyapa was also like this:
although he has not yet truly attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* today, he has already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that he shall become a Buddha in the future, and his name is...
The Buddha is the realization of one's own nature. What is called the "perfect lunar orb of the bodhisattva's mind" has fifteen phases.

For those who practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), it is the application of great compassion; it transforms the mind of stinginess and greed, enriching one's own virtue and bringing benefit and grace to all sentient beings.
The Perfection of Precepts (Śīla-pāramitā) consists of the essential function of the nature of ritual propriety: it transforms the mind of evil, strengthens oneself, and sustains sentient beings.

The Perfection of Patience (Kṣānti-pāramitā) consists of the essential function of great sincere faith: it transforms the mind of anger, guards one’s own path, and brings peace and stability to sentient beings.

The Perfection of Diligence (Vīrya-pāramitā) consists of the essential function of principle: it transforms the mind of indolence, diligently cultivates oneself, and encourages the progress of others.

The perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is the function of great wisdom; it restrains the mind from negligence, brings oneself under mastery, and brings sentient beings under mastery.
The perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the merit of the nature of knowledge and artistry; it transforms the deluded mind, brings oneself to clarity, and brings sentient beings to clarity.

The perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is the merit of the nature of benevolent wisdom; it transforms obstructive minds, making it easy to cultivate one's own path and easy to cultivate [the path of others].

Regarding those who follow their own path and vow to deliver others: through the power of their nature of benevolence and courage, they transform and eliminate the loss of mind, thereby accomplishing their own path and accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

Regarding those who rely on the power of liberation: through the power of their nature of wisdom and courage, they transform and eliminate timidity and weakness, relying instead upon abiding in their own self.

Abiding freely among sentient beings, those who know the Perfection of Wisdom realize the merit of the Great Enlightenment-nature. They transform the deluded mind, awakening to themselves and awakening to all sentient beings.
Those who possess such wisdom manifest the virtues of responsive transformation; they transform the five preceding consciousnesses to become the Buddha within themselves.

To become a Buddha for all sentient beings: the one of wondrous contemplative wisdom (prajñā) attains the merit of awakening through others' reception and transforms the sixth consciousness to become the Buddha-self.

To become a Buddha for all sentient beings: the one of equalizing wisdom attains the merit of awakening through self-reception and transforms the consciousnesses of self and person to become the Buddha-self.

Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood for sentient beings: the Great Perfect Wisdom (mahāmaṇḍala-jñāna) is the virtue of self-nature awakening; it transforms the ālayavijñāna to achieve Buddhahood for oneself and for all sentient beings.

Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood for sentient beings: the Dharma-realm Wisdom (dharmadhātu-jñāna) is the virtue of Dharma-body awakening; it transforms the ignorance-consciousness (avidyā-vijñāna) to achieve Buddhahood for oneself.

Becoming a Buddha for all sentient beings, awakening the transformation of ignorance, and realizing the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—this is called the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.

These fifteen paths are primordially and intrinsically possessed; this is called the nature of mind (*cittaprakṛti*), and this is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). When these fifteen are perfected, they are complete.

It cannot be resolved as being either identical or different; it has no beginning and no end, like a circle without a seam. It is only through skillful means that its beginning and end are taught and shown.

As for the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), although it exists, it does not manifest, just like the moon during the dark fortnight; though the wheel exists, there is no awareness of it. This refers to those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
When one first perceives the essence of nature, it is like the new moon, manifesting but a single fraction of light.

For a practitioner, wisdom and delusion coexist, like the crescent moon, half white and half black. As for the sage whose nature is realized, wisdom and vision are fully cultivated, like the full moon on the fifteenth day, its orb complete and its light perfect. Then he spoke this verse:
Ordinary beings, lacking knowledge and vision, are as dark as the moon during the new moon;
The Bodhisattvas prior to the stages have a radiance like the moon on the first day of the lunar month; The great Bodhisattvas within the stages possess a clarity like the crescent moon;
Those Bodhisattvas who have attained realization on the stages are as full as the moon on the fifteenth day. Such is this lunar orb.
This is the Tathāgata King of Certainty, named Immeasurable Life, who attained Buddhahood long ago;
he is also called the Palace of the Dharma Realm. He eternally dwells in this pure land of Constant Quiescent Light, within the lunar disc of Vairocana Buddha.
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions likewise reside together in this palace.
Neither cause nor effect, eternally abiding throughout the three periods of time— Practitioners and ordinary beings should contemplate this principle:
Sitting upright, one contemplates the lunar disc, Realizing that one’s own body is originally Vairocana Buddha;
The Dharma-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, With the crowns of the five Buddhas upon the head.

Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, wearing robes adorned with necklaces, his body the color of purple-polished gold, fully endowed with the roots of a hundred blessings, and his form adorned by ten thousand virtues;
in a single thought-moment, he knows and perceives the nature of the mind as a lunar disc; in a single thought-moment, he recollects: "My own body is the principle of Vairocana."
Such a person is named "True," a practitioner who cultivates the recollection of the Buddha.
To attain great merit, [they honor] the Buddha Akṣobhya of the East, Ratnasambhava of the South, Amitābha of the West,
and Amoghasiddhi of the North— these and immeasurable other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those who constantly recite the name, Reverently prostrate and make offerings, Throughout hundreds of thousands of years—
The merit of these individuals, And the merit of one who can measure The merit of their knowledge and vision,
Does not equal the merit of seeing the nature For even a single moment.

Even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part—none of these can equal even a single fraction [of it], let alone its eternally abiding essence, the Buddha of the fundamental nature.
Through the application of its function within the mundane and supramundane realms, it delivers the world on one hand; it liberates itself and transforms others.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Devaputra:
at that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, saying, "I have previously explained many meanings concerning the Dharma of emptiness."
This is that which can destroy numerous afflictions and accomplish the pure mind. Having already accomplished purity, one shares the empty mind of the Buddha;
this is called "becoming a Buddha. This is the first stage. Now, the moon of the mind is explained: through fifteen wondrous paths, one enters the supreme path.

This is the stage prior to attaining Buddhahood; it is able to reach the rank of Buddha, and thus constitutes the final stage. Fifteenth is "Cultivation," which is called the cause for the various ranks of Buddhas.
When this fifteenth cultivation is perfected, it is called the fruition of the Buddhas' attainment of the Way of Buddhahood.
For all sentient beings, bodily actions that correspond to these constitute the fifteen paths; the same applies to speech and mind. In all such practices, there is no evil.
It is simply good. At all times, one is without delusion and possesses only awakening. A practitioner such as this attains the body of a noble person in a single lifetime;

they are venerated by humans and devas, and offered sustenance by dragons and spirits. They travel throughout the ten directions without obstruction, without enemies, and enjoy complete peace and happiness, remaining entirely in a state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Chapter Four: The Dharma-Dhātu.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I see that the Buddhas of the dharma-dhātu are immeasurable, sentient beings are immeasurable, myriad virtues are immeasurable, and myriad evils are immeasurable. By what dharma do these become established as their basis? The Buddha—
He addressed the Great Brahma King, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O Heavenly King, you have asked well. There are seven dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) that constitute these [phenomena]:
first, the dharma-realm of the three bodies; second, the dharma-realm of the five conditions and causes; third, the dharma-realm of the four vital energies;
fourth, the dharma-realm of the seven elements; fifth, the dharma-realm of the three worlds; sixth, the dharma-realm of the four [modes of] conformity and reversal..."
The realms. Seventh, the ten realms are the dharma-realm; this is the assembly of the dharma-realm, which accomplishes all worlds.
O Heavenly King, listen attentively! What are the three aspects of the dharma-body of the dharma-realm? First, the outflow (*niṣyanda*); second, the practice of wisdom (*jñāna-caryā*);

third, the attainment of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). What are the five causes and conditions? First, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); second, ignorance (*avidyā*); third, encountering [conditions]; fourth...
...the execution. Fifth is the subsequent assembly. What are the four elemental dharmadhātus? First is the air element; second is the yang (heat) element;
third is the yin (cold) element; fourth is the life-sustaining element. What are the seven great elemental dharmadhātus? First is the earth element; second is the water element;
third is the fire element; fourth is the wind element; fifth is the space element; sixth is the consciousness element; seventh is the...
This refers to the great faculties. What is the threefold dharma-realm? First, the vessel-world; second, sentient beings; third, the five aggregates.
What is the fourfold dharma-realm of accordance and reversal? First, the five virtues; second, the ten wholesome actions;
third, the four noble truths; fourth, the six perfections. What is the tenfold dharma-realm? First, the hells; second, insentient things; third...
1. The realm of hungry ghosts; 2. The realm of hell-beings; 3. The realm of asuras; 4. The realm of animals; 5. The realm of humans; 6. The realm of celestial immortals;
7. The realm of the Two Vehicles; 8. The realm of emptiness; 9. The realm of Bodhisattvas; 10. The realm of Buddhas. What is the Dharmakāya-Dharmadhātu of the various streams?
It is the Dharmakāya-Dharmadhātu of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The principle of this Dharmadhātu gives birth to sentient beings; it is without beginning and without end, and is not...
Delusion is not awakening; this is called the *dharmadhātu* of the *dharmakāya* as natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). What is the *dharmadhātu* of the *dharmakāya* as the practice of wisdom?
It is the *dharmadhātu* of the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. As for the principle of that *dharmadhātu*, it endows all sentient beings with life; it is without beginning and without end.

When delusion transforms into awakening, this is called the *dharmadhātu* of the *dharmakāya* as the practice of wisdom. What is the *dharmadhātu* of the *dharmakāya* as the accomplishment of Buddhahood? [Vairocana...]
The Great Bhagavān Vairocana is the Great Awakening of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

As for the principle of this Dharma-realm, it is spontaneously endowed with the capacity to transform the beginningless and endless delusions of all sentient beings into awakening; this is called the Dharma-realm of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha’s realization.

What is the Dharma-realm of causal conditions of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? It is the cause that flows equally from the nature of Samantabhadra’s Dharma, which has always been so, and which conditions through contemplation.
It is the condition for the practice of the wisdom of the dharma-nature of sound; it is the cause for the practice of the wisdom of the dharma-nature of Avalokiteśvara.

It is the fruit of the dharma-nature of Vairocana, naturally conditioned by that. This is the root of the causal conditions for sentient beings. This is the dharma-realm of the causal conditions of this wondrous dharma-nature.
How is the dharma-realm of the causal conditions of ignorance? It is the primordial source of the single mind of all sentient beings. This is...

Regarding the principle of the *dharmatā*: within that wondrous and true reality of the *dharmatā*, based on the conditions of sentient beings, there suddenly arises a single thought-moment of forgetfulness;
this is the root of the transmigration of sentient beings. This is called the *dharmadhātu* of the causal condition of ignorance (*avidyā*).
How does one encounter the *dharmadhātu* of causal conditions? All sentient beings are born from the same *dharmatā*; because their entry into the *dharma* is identical, they are themselves...
However, when they meet, they encounter one another and form the conditions for birth and death. Life after life, they thus establish these karmic ties;
this nature constitutes the transmigration of sentient beings through birth and death, which is called "encountering and adhering to the dharma-realm. How does one practice the causal dharma-realm?
Because all sentient beings encounter and adhere to one another, within that state of adherence, they may give rise to compassionate love, or they may give rise to...
Whether they harbor anger and resentment, or perform wholesome deeds, or perform unwholesome deeds—these are called the karmic causes for the birth and death of sentient beings.
This is called the realm of dharmas of the causal conditions of performing and practicing. What is the realm of dharmas of the causal conditions of subsequent meeting?

All sentient beings form karmic connections in this life; by virtue of these conditions, they will necessarily attain a future birth and will likewise encounter the creation of karma. This is the birth of sentient beings.
Death lasts for eternal kalpas; this is called the *dharmadhātu* of the causes and conditions of the subsequent assembly.
How does the vital air (*prāṇa*) constitute the worldly *dharmadhātu*? Within the great emptiness that is without beginning or end, there exists a wondrous vital air without beginning or end;
this is the *tathāgatagarbha*. It contains all subtle principles and is able to serve as the source for the accomplishment of the world.
This is called the world-dharmadhātu formed by the air element. What is the world-dharmadhātu formed by the fire element? The air element transforms to produce the primary moving dharmas:
one [unit] of water in the north, three of wood in the east, five of earth in the center, and seven of fire in the south.
Nine golds in the west. Proceeding in this manner, one accomplishes the mundane world. This is called the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) of the world accomplished through yang-energy.
What is the realm of phenomena of the world accomplished through yin-energy? Yang-energy undergoes transformation and presides over the dharma of death and quiescence. Two fires in the south.
Metal is four in the west; water is six in the north; wood is eight in the east; earth is ten in the center. Following such numerical progression, the world is accomplished.
This is called the accomplishment of the world-dharmadhātu through yin-qi. What is the generation of yang-qi? The father’s qi for one month.

The vital energies (*prāṇa*) of the father and mother form the constituent parts of the sentient being’s body. During the first month, the father’s energy forms the kidneys, while at that same time, the mother’s energy forms the bladder.
During the second month, the mother’s energy can form the network of the heart, while at that same time, the father’s energy can form the small intestine.

During the third month, the father’s energy can form the liver and the mouth, while at that same time, the mother’s energy can form the gallbladder and the brain. During the fourth month, the mother’s energy can...
The father’s vital energy forms the liver and the mouth. At that time, the father’s energy is able to form the stomach. The father’s energy, in the fifth month, accomplishes the lungs and the mouth;

at that time, the mother’s energy accomplishes the major membranes (*mahā-kośa*). The father’s energy, in the sixth month, forms the bones and the ears; the mother’s energy, in the seventh month, fills the blood.
The father’s energy, in the eighth month, forms the eyes and the mother’s sinews. The mother’s energy, in the ninth month, forms the flesh and the lips. The father’s energy, in the tenth [month]...

The skin, flesh, and nose are formed by the element of water (*āpa-dhātu*). Although they are formed simultaneously, their maturation differs; this is called the world-element of the formation of the life-force.
What is the world-element of the solid substance of the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*)? The major limbs of sentient beings, the physical substance of bone and flesh—all these are the earth-element;
this is called the world-element of the earth-element of the bodily parts. What is the world-element of the moist substance of the water-element (*ap-dhātu*)? The [limbs] of sentient beings...
The body’s blood and warmth are all the water element; this is called the dharma-realm of the water element within the constituent parts of the body.
What is the dharma-realm of the fire element as warmth? The warmth of the limbs and the vital heat of sentient beings are all the fire element;

this is called the dharma-realm of the fire element within the constituent parts of the body. What is the dharma-realm of the wind element as movement? The limbs of sentient beings move according to thought.

The throbbing is entirely the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*); this is called the great dharma-realm of the wind element within the constituent parts of the body. What is the great dharma-realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*)?

Within the viscera of all sentient beings, where the qi and blood circulate through the channels, there is entirely the space element; this is called the great dharma-realm of the space element within the constituent parts of the body.
What is the dharma-realm of the consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*), the soul and spirit (*po-hun*)? It is the mind and body of sentient beings—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body...

Within the mind, the conditioned serves as the master of its locus; knowing that the spiritual consciousness is entirely the element of consciousness—this is called the Great Dharma-realm of Body, Mind, and Consciousness.

How is it that the sense organs are the great clarity penetrating the Dharma-realm? Within the loci of the sense organs of sentient beings—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the organs themselves are the element of the organ—this is called the Great Dharma-realm of Body, Mind, and Organs. What is the world of the vessel-realm?
The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The place where all sentient beings dwell, the realm of heaven and earth—this is called the world of the vessel-realm (bhājanaloka-dharmadhātu).
What is the world of the sentient-realm (sattvaloka-dharmadhātu)? All categories of beings, whether sentient or insentient, deluded or awakened—this is called the world of the sentient-realm.
What is the world of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha-loka-dharmadhātu)? It refers to the bodies of all sentient beings.

This is form (*rūpa*). "Mind" (*citta*) refers to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). These are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the mundane realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

What are the five virtues of the dharma-realm in its forward and reverse order? As for the five virtues: first, filial piety toward one's father; second, filial piety toward one's mother; third, loyalty toward one's sovereign and teacher;
fourth, assisting the sages; and fifth, taking refuge in the Triple Gem. As for the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*): first, killing...
First, killing one’s father; second, killing one’s mother; third, murdering a sovereign or teacher; fourth, killing a noble being (ārya); fifth, destroying the Triple Gem.

These are called the five transgressions of the dharma-realm in its forward and reverse order. What is the dharma-realm of the ten wholesome actions in its forward and reverse order? As for the ten in their forward order:
First, releasing living beings; second, right giving; third, moderation and chastity; fourth, truthful speech; fifth, righteous speech;
sixth, commendatory speech; seventh, harmonious speech; eighth, generous relinquishment; ninth, concordant kindness; tenth, clear wisdom.
As for the ten transgressions: first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech;
fifth, frivolous speech; sixth, harsh speech; seventh, divisive speech; eighth, covetousness; ninth, malice; [and tenth, wrong view].
The tenth is delusion. These are called the ten wholesome factors of the dharma-realm in both direct and reverse order.
What is the dharma-realm of suffering experienced in the hells? Beneath this great earth, within the limits of the golden wheel, there is a gathering of malevolent spirits.
In that world, all sentient beings who are born there are devoured and eaten by great ghosts; their births are likewise the same.
Beneath the limit of the golden wheel is a wheel of water-ice, and beneath the limit of the water-wheel is a wheel of fiery flames.
At the limit of the water-wheel and within the limit of the fire-wheel, all sentient beings are frozen by the ice and scorched by the fire, day and night without ceasing.
They undergo great suffering from poison; this is called the dharma-realm of experiencing suffering in hell. What is the dharma-realm of insentient, deluded, and poisonous dharmas?

It refers to those who are deluded and devoid of wisdom, whose minds and thoughts are obstructed. Among the various classes of beings, they may become earth or stone, or they may become living plants and trees;
this is called the dharma-realm of extreme delusion among insentient things. What are the various ghosts—the hungry ghosts, the greedy ghosts, and the pestilence ghosts?
The various classes such as poison-demons (*viṣa-graha*), yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and so forth—these are called the realm of suffering and poison of the spirit world (*preta*).
What are the various scaly beings such as the nāgas among animals; all the feathered ones such as the garuḍas; the shelled ones such as tortoises and conchs;
the hairy ones such as lions, tigers, and wolves; and all the naked insects such as the *śiṅgiṅga*? These are called... [the realm of suffering and poison of the animal world].
The animal realm is not the true realm of the Dharma. What, then, is the true and wholesome realm of the Dharma in the human world?

It is the power of the five precepts and the power of the ten wholesome actions of the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, by which one is born into the realm of innate goodness; this is called the true and wholesome realm of the Dharma in the human world.
What, then, is the realm of wholesome bliss in the heavens? It is through the great power of the ten wholesome actions and the power of the eight dhyānas that one is born into the desire realm.
The heavens and the gods of the form realm (rūpadhātu)—these are called the dharma-realm of excellent bliss in the heavens. What are the seven greats? First, the great earth-body of soil and color;

second, the great water-essence of fluids, blood, and vital seed; third, the great fire-vapor of spiritual warmth; fourth, the great wind-wood of movement and stillness; fifth, the great space-gold of empty vapor.
These five greats divide the two paths of delusion and awakening. Each of these two paths further divides into the dependent and the...

The primary retribution of the Way of Delusion forms the dependent retribution of heaven and earth and the world; the primary retribution of the Way of Delusion forms the sentient beings of humans and devas.
The dependent retribution of the Way of Awakening forms the pure lands of the ten directions; the primary retribution of the Way of Awakening forms the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

From the six great elements of consciousness: the spirit of the wind and wood elements forms the visual consciousness; the spirit of the water and sap elements forms the auditory consciousness; the spirit of the space and gold elements...

The earth element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta) forms the nose-consciousness (ghrāṇa-vijñāna). The great spirit of the earth element forms the body-consciousness (kāya-vijñāna). The fire element is the master of the single body; therefore, it is divided into two consciousnesses.
From the spirit, the tongue-consciousness (jihvā-vijñāna) is formed. The master-spirit forms the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna). Regarding the seven great elements of the six sense organs:

the wind and wood elements, as vital breath, form the eye-organ (cakṣur-indriya); the water element, as vital breath, forms the ear-organ (śrotra-indriya); the space and gold elements, as vital breath, form the nose-organ (ghrāṇa-indriya); and the earth element, as vital breath, forms the body-organ (kāya-indriya).

The faculties (*indriya*). The fire element (*tejas*) is the sovereign of the single body; therefore, it is divided into two faculties. From *vāyu* (wind) the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*) is formed; from the mastery over wind, the mind faculty (*manendriya*) is formed. How so?
The earth-consciousness faculty element (*pṛthivī-vijñānendriya-mahābhūta*) of the Tathāgatagarbha stage is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Amitāyus-niścita-rāja.
It forms the water-consciousness faculty element as the natural outflow of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Amoghasiddhi. It forms the fire-consciousness [faculty element]...
The element of earth is the outflow of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Ratnasaṃbhava; it constitutes the wind, wood, and consciousness elements of the sense-faculties.

The element of space is the outflow of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Akṣobhya; it constitutes the gold and consciousness elements of the sense-faculties. The element of water is the outflow of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Amitāyus;
it is without beginning or end, uncreated, and unconditioned. This is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
"How do the seven great elements attain Buddhahood? The Buddha said: "Within this Sahā world-system, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of heavens and earths.
Within these, there are immeasurable worlds; within those, there are countless sentient beings.

Among them are intelligent animals who practice the path of the five precepts. Upon death, they are reborn in the human realm. Without receiving [the teachings] through their own initiative, they become commoners. Yet, they receive and uphold the practice."
Thus one becomes a great man. When a wise person practices the ten paths of wholesome action among humans, after death they will certainly be reborn as a human king.

By practicing what they have undertaken, they become a minor king; by upholding [the precepts] but not practicing them, they become a great king. This is called a bodhisattva who has first entered the path.
A bodhisattva at the stage of the ten faiths becomes an iron-wheel-turning king; a bodhisattva at the stage of the ten abidings becomes a copper-wheel-turning king.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices become silver-wheel-turning kings; Bodhisattvas of the Ten Dedications become gold-wheel-turning kings;

Bodhisattvas of the First Ground become Kings of the Four Heavenly Kings; Bodhisattvas of the Second Ground become Kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; and Bodhisattvas of the Third Ground become Kings of the Yāma Heaven.
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage become kings of Tuṣita; Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage become kings of Nirmāṇarati; Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage become kings of Vaśavartin;
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage become kings of the first dhyāna; and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage become kings of the second dhyāna.
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage become kings of the third dhyāna; Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage become kings of the fourth dhyāna.

Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi) dwell in the inner court, where they enter and cultivate the exhaustion of ignorance, and subsequently descend to the human realm to attain perfect enlightenment within.

The *Yuan* (Chapter/Section). Because it is the initial practice, in the fifth section of the *Liudapin* (Six Great Chapters), at that time Śāriputra rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words: "World-Honored One, I..."
Relying on the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, one attains great wisdom and comes to universally know all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds.

In times past, there was a Wheel-Turning King who established the True Dharma for governing the world, asserting that the bodies and minds of sentient beings are composed of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. The Tathāgata’s teaching differs from this; rather, he says:
"It is composed of space, wind, fire, water, and earth. Why is this so? The Buddha told Śāriputra: "You have asked the Tathāgata well.
Thus it was: in ages past, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, relying on the Great Holy King Mahābrahmā, spoke only of the laws regarding the formation of heaven and earth.
As for what the Seven Buddhas have taught, they saw the time when heaven and earth had not yet been formed."
To explain this matter: before these dharmas were produced, there was first the formation of the great earth; before the great earth was formed, there was the formation of the various heavens;

before the heavens of desire were formed, there was the formation of the yin and yang; before the yin and yang were formed, there was the Great Qi. This Great Qi is the existence within the Great Emptiness.
It is without beginning and without end. Herein lies the Great Dharma; likewise, this Great Dharma is without beginning and without end.
In the end, it shares the same origin as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One should know that this dharma is precisely the true principle; it is the lord of emptiness.
This is called the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) and is named the *tathāgatagarbha*. Because of this dharma, the Great Emptiness possesses vital energy (*prāṇa*);

relying on this great energy, it is able to produce yin and yang; relying on this yin and yang, the heavens above are formed; and because of the heavens above, the great earth is also formed. Because the great earth is established, [all things arise].
All sentient beings are born from these; sentient beings also rely upon those dharmas to achieve awakening. Those who achieve great awakening are called the Buddhas.
For this reason, the Seven Buddhas taught the six great elements, namely: space, wind, fire, water, earth, and consciousness. Regarding "space," it is the arising of the vital breath (*qi*);
this is named the Metal element (*kṣatriya*) and constitutes the governing organ of the lungs. "Wind" refers to the movement of the vital breath; this is named the Wood element.
Movement constitutes the Wood element; it is associated with the Liver. Earth constitutes the Soil element; it is named the Earth element and is associated with the Spleen.

Fire constitutes the Fire element; it is associated with the Heart. Water constitutes the Water element; it is associated with the Kidneys. Why is Metal not mentioned? It is because it is termed the Great Space.

This refers to the element of gold (*kāñcanagati*). It is restricted solely to substantial entities (*dravya*) and does not extend to empty space. This is because "space" extends to both emptiness and substantial entities.

Why is wood not so designated? This refers to the great element of wind (*vāyudhātu*). Wood is restricted solely to its physical substance and parts; it does not universally apply to the quality of motion.

This is because wind is universally pervasive and encompasses all physical forms. Why, then, is it not referred to as "above"? It is called the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Earth is formed from soil;
it is established by becoming great, for it relies upon the great to achieve its formation. Why, then, are they not called the five shapes, but rather the six great elements?
This means that when the five elements (pañca-mahābhūta) have formed, they constitute heaven and earth; subsequently, they pertain only to the human realm and not to what has not yet been formed.

As for the six great elements (ṣaḍ-dhātu), they encompass both before and after the formation of heaven and earth. Why is this? It is because the noble Universal Monarch (cakravartin-rāja) refers only to heaven and earth, and not to what lies beyond them.
This is because the Wheel-Turning Sage King governs only the human order and does not govern what is external. So it is with the Buddhas and Tathāgatas...

Coming to know the causes, karmic actions, retributions, and fruits of the ten realms of beings, one understands that this power of karma forms the heavens, the earth, and sentient beings, even up to the attainment of Buddhahood—namely, the beginning, middle, and end.

Therefore, the teachings are not the same. He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has said concerning the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), is it spoken erroneously or delusively?
The Buddha said, "It is not so. The Wheel-Turning Sage King is spoken of in reliance upon the Brahma Heaven; he merely governs."

In this world, those of the highest capacity ascend to heaven; those of middling capacity transform into immortals; and those of lower capacity govern human beings. These do not include those who transcend the world;

therefore, the dharmas beyond heaven and earth are not discussed here. The Buddhas of the three periods of time lead beings both within and beyond the world: those of the highest capacity attain Buddhahood;

next, they become Bodhisattvas; next, they become Pratyekabuddhas; and next, they become Śrāvakas. These are able to transcend the mundane world and attain the ranks of the sages. As for those of middling capacity—
Ascending to heaven; next, ascending to the realm of the immortals (*śramaṇa*); next, governing human beings—he is able to govern the world and establish the royal law.

Those of lower capacity are liberated from the various realms of animals; next, liberated from the hungry ghosts (*preta*); next, liberated from the hells. They are able to leave the realm of suffering and be born in the good paths (*sugati*).
For this reason, he is able to expound the True Dharma of cause and effect regarding what precedes and follows heaven. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Great..."
The Brahmā King has long lived and endured. He heard this directly from what the seven Buddhas taught. Why, then, do you ask why it was not taught by the seven Buddhas?
The Buddha said, "Excellent! It is just as you have asked. Nevertheless, that which was taught by the seven Buddhas was long since extinguished and did not circulate among humans.
At the time when a Wheel-Turning King appeared in the world at the beginning of the kalpa, although the Great Brahmā King..."
Knowing this Dharma, yet because the state of wondrous enlightenment has not been perfected, one does not fully know its laws of cause and effect;
thus, one may wait for the time when a future Buddha appears in the world to preach it, rather than preaching it now.

At the times of all past Buddhas, my present Buddha, and all future Buddhas, this Dharma of mine shall gradually spread to the various countries of the East, being disseminated in succession. The laws of those various countries shall likewise [be transformed].

It was again as before. He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how do you speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? The Buddha said, "Emptiness presides over the lungs and governs the constituent parts of the body;
it is the great element of emptiness within the nine orifices and the pores, through which the qi and blood of the six *fu* and six *zang* organs pass.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how do you speak of wind (*vāyu*)? The Buddha said, "Wind presides over the liver and governs the major movements of the heart, body, and limbs."

[The disciple] said: "All these are the element of wind. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why do you speak of fire? The Buddha said: "Fire presides over the heart organ and governs bodily warmth;
all these are the element of fire. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why do you speak of water? The Buddha said:

"Water presides over the kidney organ and governs the essence of the kidneys, as well as the major and minor limbs, blood, fat, and secretions; all these are the element of water. He addressed the Buddha...
He asked, "World-Honored One, how do you speak of earth? The Buddha said, "The spleen, the internal organs, bones, flesh, and all solid substances—these are all the earth element.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying, "World-Honored One, as for these six great elements, by what path are they maintained? Furthermore, is there cultivation of them?"
The Buddha said: "The six great elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha; they are united with the original source. The correct, virtuous awakening of this Tathāgatagarbha is called cultivation.
Those who cultivate in this way will all attain the Way of the Buddha. To turn one's back on such cultivation and to indulge in arbitrary, deluded conduct is not the path."

Such sentient beings all follow the cycle of birth and death; from life to life and age to age, they transmigrate and undergo suffering without end, like the revolving of a wheel. How pitiable they are!
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why do you say that consciousness is the master of the soul and the spirit, and the master of the gate of life?
That all vital essences and energies are the great element of consciousness? At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when the vital energy of sentient beings has been exhausted and they pass away, earth, water, fire, wind, and space all disperse and vanish. What constituent part remains within them that could enter into the intermediate state?"
[He] is reborn hereafter. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "As you have asked, the constituent parts of a sentient being depend upon the limits of karmic retribution (*vipāka*).
They arise through the mandate of destiny (*daivam*), for it is by receiving the vital breath of the parents that the physical body is formed.

When the retribution is exhausted and the limit of the mandate of destiny has reached its end at the time of death, the great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—dissolve and perish. Although these five great elements perish, the element of consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not."
It ceases. Why? Because consciousness does not exist dependent upon karmic retribution; it is not produced by life-force (*jīva*); it is not received through vital breath (*prāṇa*).
It is without beginning and without end, for it is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Consciousness takes the fundamental principles of earth, water, fire, wind, and space as its body.
The essence of emptiness exists through its dark substance; both arise based on the causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma.

Just as one’s present-life karma relies upon its respective state, one relinquishes the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space of this [current] stage, while simultaneously receiving those [new] elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space.

Furthermore, at the very moment of birth—whether through moisture, womb, egg, or transformation—one receives a corresponding birth according to one's realm and according to one's karmic retribution, taking birth within the six destinies.

This is called "transmigration through the three periods of time. May all beings take pity on this state, emerge from the human realm, and extensively explain this principle so that sentient beings may return to the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* of the six great elements, day after day.

The six great elements: at all times, the six great elements do not abandon nor forget the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*. To be able to harmonize with this principle is called the practice of the *dharmakāya* of the six great elements.
Chapter Six: Subduing Māra.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda, you should know that this sutra is truthful, difficult to believe, and difficult to practice.
It is not that those who are unsuitable for this sutra lack faith and practice; rather, this sutra is the direct path to supreme Buddhahood, and it is for those who are supreme."
There will inevitably be demonic obstacles. For this reason, it is difficult to believe and difficult to practice. What constitutes demonic activity?
There are four kinds of demons that constitute great hindrances to its widespread propagation: first, the celestial demons who create obstacles; second, external demons;

third, other demons, namely the demons of heterodox views and non-Buddhist paths; and fourth, one's own internal demons. With such obstacles as these, it is truly difficult to practice and truly difficult to cure.

As for why the celestial Māras obstruct those who rely on this sutra: there is no one who will not attain Buddhahood. For this reason, the celestial Māras constantly create hindrances and difficulties.
Even when the time arrives for its propagation throughout the world, they crosswise block it so that it does not reach the time of its propagation.
Or, even if there are people in the world who propagate it, they cause them to have no companions. Or they cause others to slander and challenge them, or they summon...
Calamities shall arise, causing suffering within that land. Or, they may take recourse in humans, declaring that this sutra was not spoken by the seven Buddhas;
or, they may claim it was propagated in the world through human speech, leading others to believe that those who propagate it are practitioners of heterodox paths.

Or, they may entrust the matter to celestial sons, kings, dukes, or high ministers, causing them to desire that this sutra not be propagated within the nation. Alas! This sutra is being obstructed by Māras and shall not be widespread.
To propagate and disseminate it widely. With my Buddha-eye, I see that this is difficult to cure;

therefore, I shall not rely on the words, letters, or phrases of the sūtras, but shall instead transmit these principles from mind to mind, causing them to be widely propagated and disseminated throughout the world through skillful means.

I shall cause Avalokiteśvara and the other great bodhisattvas to be able to preserve and uphold it. I leave this sutra scroll so that, like me, they may protect and mind it, ensuring it is never permanently severed.
Ānanda, you should know that anyone who upholds and transmits this sutra is a bodhisattva of great power.
