For the practitioner of truth, what constitutes external māras? There are two kinds: first, the māra-view of the extinction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
second, the māra-view of becoming a spirit or ghost realm. What is meant by those who study worldly learning and become practitioners of the path of the vital breath? They study worldly teachings.
One does not know that the mind creates heaven, earth, the myriad things, good and evil fruits, and even the ten realms;

yet one should understand that heaven, earth, the five elements, the myriad things, and the five types of insects among humans are all created by *qi*. When the primal *qi* disperses, the mind also disperses.

One who establishes [the view of] emptiness as non-existence and lacks the mind [of compassion] will have no future retribution; by repudiating cause and effect, such a person shall fall into the evil destinies.
Alas! This person does not understand the teaching. He who originated this teaching was a high-ranking Bodhisattva who became a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*);

appearing in the world at the proper time, he governed humanity and established the teachings through his vital energy (*prāṇa*). As for those who establish the teachings through the mind, they await the arising of the Buddha’s discourse.
Although this teaching does not assert the non-existence of mind, the absence of a self, or the lack of karmic retribution— views held by external paths—
it is because ordinary people have falsely calculated and misunderstood that, when the sacred teachings established by the Wheel-Turning Sages were lost in transmission,
they privately devised doctrines such as nihilism and the view of annihilation, falsely establishing these schools throughout this land, other lands, and even across the trichiliocosm.
The noble kings who appeared at the beginning of the eon were all high-level mahāsattva bodhisattvas.
Therefore, whatever teachings they proclaimed were free from error or falsehood; they were entirely authentic instructions, correct and virtuous, capable of governing the realm.

In accordance with the minds of the people, both in this country and other countries, at present and in the future, various followers of external paths will all establish their own private tenets to destroy my holy teaching.
They will not only destroy the teachings I have spoken, but will also destroy the doctrinal systems established and revealed by the holy kings of antiquity.
Thus, through prolonged error and the formation of false understandings, these people will at times perceive me as merely a follower of [limited] knowledge and vision.
They instead utter slander, being ignorant of the True Principle, deluded and inverted, performing useless deeds that greatly obstruct the path of refuge.
All people within the gateway of my knowledge and vision lack this sutra and its Way; why then would they study worldly learning to become divine or perfected beings?

It merely maintains the present life and does not consider future lives; it knows only that when a person dies they become a ghost or a deity, but does not know how to transcend birth and death to attain Buddhahood.
This teaching was likewise established by the Sage-King and is the purport of the holy doctrine. It prevails during times of decline in the world.

Because they have distanced themselves from the Sage, they falsely form these interpretations. Those with long-standing memories and great talents who falsely study this essential teaching do so for the sake of cultivating their own minds and bodies, not for the sake of mere scholarly memorization;
yet they fail to rectify themselves and instead only seek to refute the teachings of others. Alas!

These people likewise do not realize that this teaching was originally established by the Holy King and is no different from what was spoken by the Tathāgata; they merely perceive it through their own limited views and knowledge.

Those who claim that one becomes a Buddha through human effort slander the Way of the True Nature of Heaven, asserting that there is no attaining Buddhahood within the Palace of the Dharma-realm, nor any Buddhas dwelling in the Pure Lands of the ten directions, nor any evil-doers residing in hell—all such claims are false words.
To form such views while failing to understand this principle is the mark of a most foolish person; it obstructs those who would turn toward the truth.
What are the four types of māras encountered within the interpretation of the scriptures? There are four: first, the māra of extensive learning in words and letters;

second, the māra of the view of essentialism through equal ignorance; third, the māra of the view of attachment to signs regarding easy practices; and fourth, the māra of the view of attachment to signs regarding difficult practices.
What is the māra of extensive learning in words and letters? It is the śramaṇa who clings to the literal text regarding all that I have taught.
Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras, having exhausted all treasuries and all sections, they analyze the words and phrases, compose commentaries and transmissions, lecture upon them and explain them;
yet they clarify only the literal meanings of the characters, chapters, and sentences, claiming, "I possess great wisdom, vast learning, and a powerful memory;

I have mastered the meaning of all sūtras and am free from ignorance. They do not know that the true principles of those sūtras are all within their own minds. As for what is spoken in the various sūtras...
As for "speaking," it refers to articulating one's own mental principles rather than the meaning of the words; it is an excess of learning and an excess of talent.

It establishes the self and pride, thereby subverting my teaching and plunging deeply into deviant paths to become companions of Māra. Hearing spoken words and taking them to be the Buddha’s speech, yet examining the mental interpretation of their principles and finding them to be external Māras—how tragic that such a person does not know that the Buddhas appear in the world to preach the Dharma and transform beings through teaching!

The essential meaning is this: if one does not awaken to the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and does not practice to accomplish the cultivation that extinguishes ordinary karma and accomplishes the cultivation of noble karma, nor practice to extinguish ordinary breaths and accomplish the cultivation of noble breaths, then even if one possesses extensive learning, great talent, and eloquence, what benefit would there be in the Tathāgata appearing in the world to preach the Dharma?
Such a foolish person, though they may claim to see the truth, does not establish it in writing.
To say that one who knows and perceives the nature of the mind is a person who acts as a Buddha is a grave slander;

it is to label such a person a follower of Māra and to utterly obstruct their turning toward the path of this sutra and all its practices. Such deluded people are difficult for the Buddhas of the three periods of time to cure.

Among all people, there is not a single Buddha nor a single Bodhisattva who merely understands the letters of the text or merely maintains extensive learning, yet fails to awaken to the nature of the mind and fails to cultivate the path of awakening—those who have already attained the Buddha-way or are destined to attain the Buddha-way.
Such foolish people are not my disciples; they are the followers of Māra. What is the essential summary? To see Māra through folly is to be a person of no wisdom.
Regarding the gateways within the various teachings and sūtras I have spoken, they take up a single essential passage and become deeply attached to its principle.

They completely abandon other teachings, asserting that these profound dharma-gates are neither true nor the essential path. Discerning "this" as right and "that" as wrong, they discard everything else.
Day by day their faith increases, yet they cling to their own false views; from time to time their sense of revulsion toward the vast path of the Buddhas grows ever stronger.
They cling [to their views] and enter darkness in succession, abandoning wisdom and abandoning insight, until they finally become utterly deluded.

Even if the Buddhas appear to shatter this perversion, or if the great Bodhisattvas shatter this folly, these people do not hear or enter [the truth], but instead give rise to anger and perversity, and even commit great slander, saying, "You do not know;
you are falsely destroying my Dharma. When they encounter this sutra, those who possess knowledge and vision regard them as being lost.
People do not understand the essential Dharma; they falsely construct their own intellectual interpretations. The Buddhas perceive them as such;

this is known as the path of views. It is vast and of no benefit. How could a fool ever be able to understand it? Even if one were able to understand it, what would it avail to show it to the heavens?
It only leads to the abandonment of true knowledge and views, causing entry into the evil realms. Such teaching obstructs my Great Way. Alas! These people do not know the Buddhas.
The practice brings about fulfillment. All Bodhisattvas increase their wisdom in every birth and attain the principle in every life;

they benefit beings at the beginning of each eon and manifest awakening in every generation. Thus, the Buddhas truly deliver these foolish people out of compassion for them. Ānanda, you should know this.

If such a foolish person should obtain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and manifest the signs of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), these are merely the works performed by a celestial Māra who has come to transform them;
do not give rise to even a single thought of faith or trust. Such a foolish person is truly difficult to cure.

Among all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all Bodhisattvas, there is not a single one—not even a single Bodhisattva—who does not penetrate all principles through the meaning of a single phrase.
Holding onto a single essential passage while failing to understand the Way of Nature, one abandons wisdom and becomes foolish;
being entirely devoid of spiritual capacity, such a person has already failed to realize the Buddha-way, or will fail to do so. Such a fool is not my disciple, but rather a follower of Māra.
Why? Because they are weak śramaṇas who, while reciting various sūtras and teachings I have spoken to transform the ignorant, remain attached to signs and encounter Māra.
Those who lack the roots of virtue may rely upon the skillful means of the Buddhas of the past, yet they still cannot find rest.

Even if one establishes skillful teachings—whether by taking refuge in a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva, or by upholding a single mantra or a single phrase from a sutra—one must take refuge in them and place faith in them.
They do not rely on difficult practices to extinguish sins or neutralize poisons, nor do they establish a path through skillful means.

There may be śramaṇas of inferior faculties who have broken the precepts and grow weary of cultivating the true path of the various sages and holy ones. Like those who have obtained a boat for crossing over, they see this [path] and rejoice;

they completely abandon the path of the Buddhas’ precepts and wisdom, adhering exclusively to this path of skillful means. They do not know that the Buddhas cannot be attained by stopping here. Even if they just barely...
At that time, the path of expedient means—the provisional and temporary way—takes these very provisional expedients as the supreme dharma, calling it the "Unsurpassed Path.

Alternatively, harboring perverse thoughts, they claim, "I am one who can attain all paths for people," yet they have not seen nor attained the supreme, wondrous Dharma or the most excellent, wondrous path.
They attract various foolish people and, for the sake of those fools, establish lectures and assemblies, expounding upon them extensively.
He expounded extensively, declaring that this path is the most supreme and most exquisite, such that only by following this single route can sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
He asserted that all other sutra paths are difficult to practice and that all ordinary persons possess inferior faculties;

thus, among hundreds of thousands of millions of people with inferior faculties who rely on the path of difficult practice, not even one person in reality could ever attain the path to Buddhahood. In this regard—

All demonic spirits, having found an opportunity, increase their power and strength; because they secretly provide assistance, they cause his faith and spirit to grow day by day, and they also cause the flow of their own heterodox teachings to expand and spread day by day. Furthermore, all foolish people, deluded by worldly customs, [benefit] from this merit.

I am now fortunate enough to have the honor of submitting this great work. Why is this? Because all foolish people delight in evil and loathe virtuous deeds, being indolent in the practice of goodness.

Nevertheless, all the worthy sages and all the Buddhas—both those who have already spoken and those who speak now—declare that one who commits evil is neither a human being nor a follower of the Buddha.
Such a person, having committed transgressions and incurred harm, will be reborn in the evil realms in a future life. Thus it is said:
In life after life, one will receive evil retributions, forever severing the great path to attaining Buddhahood and liberation.

For this reason, one should abandon complacency and indolence, and diligently cultivate practice by relying on ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). One should cultivate the perfections (*pāramitā*), endure hardships, and bear suffering, relying upon the teachings of the noble trainings.

Fearing transgression, one abandons evil and proceeds toward the noble path. Yet now, having encountered these teachings that are easy to practice, if one does not rely upon the traces of the sages...
By relying on the Noble Path, one is forever freed from the evil realms and directly attains Buddhahood; this is a source of great celebration and joy.

Yet all these people follow this teaching and thereby immediately abolish the True Dharma of all Buddhas. It is not only my method for attaining Buddhahood that they abolish, but they also abolish the royal law, benevolence, righteousness, and the Noble Path.
Why is this? Because it causes the minds of all people to become deeply attached to easy practices, such that they do not understand the underlying principles.

For this reason, [if one were to] personally commit sins, personally commit transgressions, personally fall into delusion, personally engage in falsehood, personally act with evil, personally follow what is heterodox, or treat one's father,
mother, ruler, minister, sages, worthies, Heaven, and one's own life as distant strangers— how could this not naturally cause the abandonment of the Holy Path?
Those false śramaṇas, upon seeing this sūtra and those who know and see the Way, will harbor great malice toward them and slander them, saying:

"These practitioners do not know the direct path; they are long lost in delusion and create obstacles for the practice of the Way. Those who know and see the Way are difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
they are utterly unsuited for the ignorant and foolish people of this turbid and evil age. Among thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of such people, [they will speak thus].
To claim that there is no delusion within the Middle Way and that one achieves this path [thereby] is truly laughable.

This false teaching has spread throughout the world, greatly obstructing those who enter the way of knowledge and vision. Alas! These people do not understand the intent behind the skillful means established by the Buddhas.

The Buddhas establish this path of skillful means with the intention of first instructing them; taking this as a condition, they cause them to give rise to faith and draw near to the Buddha, gradually increasing all seeds of Buddhahood, leading them into the Buddha-way, and opening, revealing, awakening, and entering them into the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This enables them to attain Buddhahood. Ānanda, you should know that those who mindfully recollect the Triple Gem possess a boat or raft upon the middle path leading to the place of the treasure of knowledge and vision.
Yet these foolish people, failing to recognize the boat or raft, instead grasp hold of it and thereby block their own way to the place of the treasure.
Truly, this is to be lamented. This name does not negate the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; rather, it negates one's own path of recollecting the Triple Gem.

Why is this? Whether it be recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, or recollection of the Sangha—though these are all indeed the teachings spoken by the Buddhas—they become objects of "false recollection" for the minds of foolish śramaṇas. Thus, they [mis]recite the Dharma of the Triple Gem.

They thereby establish false dharmas. Because they cultivate false dharmas, they fall into the path of Māra. Because they themselves fall into the path of Māra, they cause others to fall into it as well.
Both their own downfall and that of others destroy the Buddha-dharma. Because they destroy the Buddha-dharma, they destroy their mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
How could they merely fall among the ranks of the demonic and heterodox? In the end, they will fall into the great fiery pit of the Avīci hell for immeasurable and boundless kalpas.
For an interval, they undergo immeasurable suffering and forever sever the seed of the Buddha. Such foolish people are truly difficult to cure.

Among all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all Bodhisattvas, there is not a single Buddha nor a single Bodhisattva who did not rely on this sutra to realize the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To mind one Tathāgata, to mind one phrase of the sutra, or to mind one Bodhisattva—this is solely the One Practice; by it, one has already attained Buddhahood.
"The Path. One shall attain the Buddha-way. Such a foolish person is not my disciple; they are a follower of Māra.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how can such a foolish person escape the magic of Māra and his followers? "They should return to faith in the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, such a foolish person should immediately cease their arrogance and turn their mind back toward reflection. They should think: 'I am...'"
"I am a fool; I am an evil person who shall fall into the fiery pits of the three miserable realms.

Yet, there are the Buddhas, who, through their great compassion, are able to employ skillful means for our sake and teach this path of easily practiced mindfulness of the Three Jewels, so that I, a fool, may forever leave the three miserable realms behind.
That I still have such a remnant of merit as this, and that I shall go to the Pure Land, is truly not [unjustified]."
Reflecting upon my own capacity for the skillful means of the Dharma, I shall no longer contend with others regarding the supreme path.
Thinking thus, I shall either recollect the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, or the Sangha Jewel; focusing exclusively upon whichever Jewel I contemplate, I shall have no other thoughts or pursuits.
Relying on my inferior faculties, I lack the means to attain the supreme path; therefore, I take refuge solely in the path of the Tathāgata’s skillful means. Regarding myself...
Regarding other phenomena: there is neither right nor wrong, and one does not obstruct the paths of others. One turns solely toward oneself to sweep away the defilements of the mind.

When one desires to focus exclusively on recitation, the various māras will retreat. The Three Jewels will manifest; since one is without fault and others are likewise without fault, this immediately constitutes my teaching.

If, while recollecting the Dharma of the Three Jewels for even a single moment, one gives rise to a mind of *adhimāna*—pride that views oneself as superior and others as inferior—it conversely acts as [an obstacle].

The conduct of Māra is likewise the departure from the conduct of the Buddhas. Even regarding the path of the Buddhas’ true knowledge and vision, to claim that one is superior and others are inferior is itself the path of Māra. Why is this? This knowledge and vision of the Buddhas is for the sake of attaining Buddhahood;

it is not for the sake of giving rise to a mind of pride by seeing oneself as superior and others as inferior. How much more so regarding those inferior practices which are merely the skillful means for cultivating Buddhahood!
Thus, one considers oneself superior to others who follow the path of excellence. What constitutes difficult practice? It is the attachment to signs and the vision of Māra.
There are śramaṇas within my Dharma who are extremely wicked, extremely foolish, and extremely perverse;
they are icchantikas, born blind, and born deaf. Even the spiritual powers of all Buddhas and the power of all Bodhisattvas cannot reach them. This is because [the Buddha], when compared with them...
Then, he performed an exquisite and inconceivable rite, using divine mantras to empower all sinners so that they might attain liberation.
By the very nature of this mantra-rite, ten kinds of merit arise spontaneously. What are these ten?
First, ordinary beings are transformed into holy sages (*ṛṣi*). Second, evil deeds are transformed into virtuous qualities. Third, ignorance is transformed into understanding.
1. Liberation; 2. Transformation of the cycle of rebirth into the attainment of birth in the Pure Land; 3. Transformation of demonic obstacles into the deeds of the sages;
4. Transformation of illness and affliction into peace and security; 5. Transformation of premature death into longevity; 6. Transformation of natural disasters into divine blessings;
7. Transformation of enemies into benevolent companions; 8. Transformation of military turmoil into tranquility and stability; and the rest... [furthermore].
There are immeasurable divine manifestations. This practitioner of incantations undergoes difficult practices and ascetic austerities, and various divine manifestations appear before him.
Whether it be those with perverse thoughts, those of dull faculties, fools, or those driven by profit and desire, he becomes their refuge for the world;

or for those who delight in miracles, he enters the mountain forests for the sake of miraculous arts, practicing various difficult austerities such as bathing in water and subsisting on roots, thereby attaining great spiritual power.

These [teachings] appear in the world and startle all people; they claim that this dharma is the most supreme and excellent among all the Buddhas' teachings, yet they lead the populace onto deviant paths.
Failing to recognize what has been established as the Tathāgata’s skillful means, they take pleasure only in all manner of strange and delusive matters.
Forever submerged in false views, they fall entirely into the way of Māra and will ultimately surely fall into the fires of the three miserable realms.
This pitfall is not only strange in itself; it causes those of heterodox paths to lose the True Way, and in turn causes the Way of the Buddhas and Great Sages to appear collectively strange.

That the Dharma lacks its true path is truly lamentable. Ānanda, you should know that when the Buddhas and Tathāgatas establish these expedient and spiritually efficacious methods, the primary purpose is to enable the rescue of those whose sins are otherwise difficult to save. They can indeed deliver them.
This is the entry into the gates of liberation. Therefore, the Buddhas established the first five merits as the primary reality.
The second set is also established for the sake of compassion, so that in the present life the world may be peaceful and the myriad people may be at ease;
thus, the latter five merits are established as secondary. That the remaining [merits] are efficacious is entirely due to the natural power and efficacy of the mantras. This is spontaneous.
Fools become attached to various strange and miraculous signs that are useless for their reputation, thereby forgetting their original intent to realize Buddhahood as a practical verification.
What benefit is there in such things as making water flow uphill, moving mountains, binding spirits with incantations, or turning water into boiling broth?
These matters do nothing but result in actual liberation [from suffering]. A śramaṇa who possesses the Way causes the waters of a nation to flow backward and brings harm to people.
As for those bound by demonic incantations, because these are beneficial, they are themselves acts of Buddha-work.
Apart from such arts, when those who rely on heterodox verifications see this sutra, they—knowing and seeing the path—instead engage in slander, claiming there is no merit or virtue.

They say that the practitioner of the Way is foolish, not realizing that they themselves possess merit and virtue, and that [the practitioner] is practicing a powerless, inferior, and shallow path that greatly obstructs all Buddhas.
This is the true and correct Dharma. Such foolish people are truly difficult to cure.

Among all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all the Bodhisattvas, there is not a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva who did not rely upon knowledge and vision to attain the right path to Buddhahood; they never cultivated that which yields no beneficial result.
Those who have already attained the Buddha-way, and those who shall attain the Buddha-way—such foolish people are not my disciples; they are the followers of Māra.

What is meant by "knowing and seeing the divergent paths and the obstacles of Māra"? There shall be ten categories. The first is that one practicing dhyāna-sitting must not fall under the influence of delusive Māras.
Second is the demon of delusion regarding discernment and lack of awakening; third is the demon of failing to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy;

fourth is the demon of failing to manifest insight due to apprehension of difficulty; fifth is the demon of losing one's way through apprehension of ease; sixth is the demon of insight that is known but not cultivated.
Seventh is the demon-view of being able to cultivate [the path] while failing to perceive delusion. Eighth is the demon-view of perceiving emptiness yet not falling into delusion therein.
Ninth is the demon-view of perceiving cessation as unreal. Tenth is the demon-view of differing perceptions regarding mental instruction. There are immeasurable such demon-views of this kind.
I have merely briefly indicated these ten types of demons for the scholar to examine, so that you may not fall into them. Why would one who sits in meditation fall into the delusion of demons?
It is because those on the path of the One Vehicle, in order to progress toward knowledge and vision, practice meditative concentration as a form of spiritual cultivation.
From morning until evening, and from evening until dawn, one practices only empty meditation. After many days and many years, one gradually realizes that there is nothing;
the mind becomes tranquil and empty, free of perception and thought. Seeing this emptiness, one enters it as the path of Buddha-nature.

Within my dhyāna, I have attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; because I have nothing further to look back upon, I do not know that those who follow the path of the Buddhas’ knowledge and vision take the mind to be holy, wise, awakened, or the principle—merely regarding the essence of empty stillness as one aspect of knowledge, which is yet not ultimate reality.

Having practiced and cultivated the concentrated mind for such a long time, one attains stillness within meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Yet, because this is not the true Buddha-nature, there is no stillness at the moment of its arising;

thus, while within absorption, the mind arises as still, empty, and pure, yet at the time of absorption, the mind disperses. This occurs whenever a person in the human realm enters or emerges from absorption;
the differentiation of the mind is not unique to this state alone. Furthermore, being deluded, one does not realize that the mind has dispersed. This is...
Because they rely on an inability to attain true knowledge and vision, their minds revert to mere distraction. This is because their cultivation of dhyāna has not yet been refined;
therefore, they further cultivate the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). Following this practice, they enter into emptiness and perceive only absolute voidness.

They fail to attain the path of the Buddha’s true knowledge and vision. Students must understand this and avoid falling into this demonic state. If one mistakenly enters it, even after passing through kalpas, one will not attain knowledge and vision. This is the work of Māra.

I fear this demon. Why do you distinguish and discern without awakening to the delusive demon? You who follow the path of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) should look upon great beings such as Vimalakīrti, who dwell in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), whose eloquence is vibrant and active, and who are unimpeded and sovereign. You should contemplate and know that their eloquence is wondrous because it is the activity of the nature of seeing;

yet you instead focus exclusively on substituting for them in verbal discernment. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you should practice only the vitality of eloquence for a long time.

By practicing it, one ultimately attains refinement and reaches mastery. Yet, if one thinks only of oneself having attained the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas and claims mastery while disregarding principle—such that principle does not recognize the path of the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas—that is truly sincere, refined, tranquil, and virtuous;
however, this is merely the virtue of discerning capacities, a single aspect of knowledge and vision, and is not yet the ultimate reality.
Ten Demonic Obstructions of Vital Energy Governing by Celestial Spirits: 1. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for high intelligence combined with broken precepts.

2. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for upholding precepts while disparaging wisdom. 3. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for attachment to wonders while practicing meditative concentration. 4. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for four types of views regarding wisdom and precepts. 5. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for relying on treasures while acting contrary to the Dharma. 6.

The demonic obstruction of the retribution for having subtle understanding yet remaining without [true] realization. 7. The demonic obstruction of the retribution for arrogance in one's wisdom and conduct. 8. Having wisdom but lacking... [text fragment].

1. The demon of retribution for one's essential nature; 2. The demon of retribution for deceiving people through the nine outward displays of learning; 3. The demon of retribution for delighting in long-winded disquisitions on the wheel [of dharma];

4. The two demons that obstruct with externalist false views: a. The demon of the view that the vital breath returns to extinction; b. The demon of the view that attaining spiritual powers yields no fruit; 5. The four demons that obstruct with erroneous interpretations within the [Buddhist] explanation:
a. The demon of the view that true insight lies in extensive textual scholarship; b. The demon of the view that true insight lies in concise summaries of texts; c. The demon of ease...
1. The demon of weariness and aversion toward practice. 2. The demon of seeing the four difficult practices as strange. 3. The demon of obstacles to knowing and seeing the divergent paths. (10) 4.

The demon of becoming deluded because one cannot attain the meditative seat. 5. The demon of being deluded by failing to awaken despite possessing analytical discernment. 6. The demon of seeing no distinction between the ordinary and the sage.

1. The delusive māra of not giving rise to contemplation regarding the four foundations of mindfulness; 2. The delusive māra of easy differentiation regarding the five faculties; 3. The delusive māra of failing to cultivate insight and vision; 4.
The delusive māra of being unable to see while practicing cultivation; 5. The delusive māra of failing to penetrate emptiness through one's views;
6. The delusive māra of viewing cessation as unreal; 7. The delusive māra of the mind and its teachings being discordant.
Chapter Seven: On Rebirth.

[A disciple] addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, throughout the sutras spoken during more than forty years, you have constantly taught that one should maintain mindfulness of and recite the names of Buddhas—such as Bhaisajyaguru Buddha and Amitābha Buddha—mindfully recollecting them with the mind and vocally invoking them with the tongue. What merit is obtained thereby?"
"Virtue. The Buddha said, "The Heavenly King has four meanings: first, drawing near to the Great Sage; second, aspiring to and delighting in the path of the Sage;
third, receiving the assistance of the Sage; and fourth, entering through the conditions of the Sage. By such meanings, his merit is said to be great.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, you have further spoken of constantly mindful recollection of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī..."
"Regarding the Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Maitreya, how is it so? The Buddha said, "O Heavenly King, listen.
When one contemplates Avalokiteśvara, this Bodhisattva gives rise to great wisdom through the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. The essence of that wisdom is great compassion;
that compassionate mind is itself the great vows and practices. This is the very body of the path of all Buddhas, and for all sentient beings it is likewise thus."
Practicing the Way: by recollecting Mañjuśrī, one attains great wisdom; by recollecting Samantabhadra, one enters into the great vows and practices;
by recollecting Maitreya, one attains the wisdom of great compassion. This practice of compassion is the great framework of the Buddha-way.

The Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, the Buddhas of the future, and the Buddhas of the east, west, south, north, above, and below, along with their Great Dharma—[are all contained herein].
First, entering the practice of compassion and wisdom. Among the Buddha-dharma, there is not a single Tathāgata who attained Buddhahood apart from the practice of wisdom;
there is not a single sentient being who shall attain Buddhahood without the practice of compassion and wisdom.

If one were to say that there is a method for attaining Buddhahood outside of the practice of wisdom and compassion, this is the teaching of external paths (tīrthikas) and not the teaching of the Seven Buddhas. All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—[are thus unified] by this one...
All Bodhisattvas practice the conduct of wisdom and compassion through difficult and arduous practices to deliver themselves and transform others.
There is not a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva who has already attained the Way of Buddhahood or will attain it without personally practicing the path of wisdom and compassion;

none have attained the Way of Buddhahood by relying on the power of another Buddha or another Bodhisattva. If one were to say that there is such a thing as attaining success without practicing these merits oneself, relying [on another], [it would be false].
"Attaining the Buddha-way through other-power is the teaching of Pāpīyān; it is not the teaching of the Buddha. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what reason do one cultivate various meritorious virtues, contemplate the Buddha, and recite his name to be reborn in the Pure Land? What is the cause of this?"

The Buddha said to the Heavenly King: "Bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve and those of inferior faculties feel great terror in this Sahā world while practicing the six perfections and myriad deeds, as well as cultivating the path of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Some may become weary and exhausted; others may regress."

By means of the Buddha’s skillful means, he returns from the accomplishment of the faculties and powers in the Pure Land to this world in order to bring the great practice of the ten thousand virtues to fulfillment;
for this purpose, he expounds this teaching. Among those practitioners of such a kind, there are two types of capacities:

first, those who gain the benefit of the supreme meaning in this present life; second, those who gain the benefit of an inferior capacity in a future life. What constitutes gaining the benefit in this present life?

This is a supreme opportunity. From the very beginning, those with sharp faculties and quick intelligence, upon opening their vision to the path of the sutras, immediately understand that the Buddhas Amitābha and our Śākyamuni established their vows and gave instructions to exhort beings toward rebirth. This is precisely the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas.
This is why they do not stop; it is to explain the truth so as to cause all sentient beings to practice the Great Way of Samantabhadra.
Without seeking rebirth elsewhere, they proceed directly toward the Great Way of Samantabhadra and thereby become Bodhisattvas of Great Capacity.
There may be bodhisattvas who, for the sake of rebirth, when contemplating the Buddha’s body, clearly perceive their own bodies as being the Buddha.
Upon awakening to this principle, they suddenly realize that the time and place of this land are entirely pure lands; without changing this very body, it is itself the Buddha-body.
They realize this immediately and achieve the faculties and powers without relying on rebirth; only then is their true practice perfected. There may be bodhisattvas...

O Śāriputra, for those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) in order to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], it is not possible to fully possess the ten great minds of mindfulness.
As previously answered in response to the questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva, these ten mindfullnesses are the fundamental mindfulness practiced by all bodhisattvas.

For the sake of mindfulness of the Buddha, they constantly cultivate the ten mindfullnesses. One who penetrates through each and every thought-moment into these ten mindfullnesses shall immediately attain [it].

They accomplish the great practices of a bodhisattva without depending on rebirth, directly cultivating the myriad virtues. Alternatively, there may be bodhisattvas who, for the sake of rebirth, cultivate the three minds:
they are without violence, without distraction, and without confusion; they are without defilement and without deviance—this constitutes the attainment of the mind of utmost sincerity.
Regarding the characteristics of that mind, it is without falsehood, without deception, without guile, without delusion, without doubt, and without greed or anger. This is...

Generosity is this precept; it is wisdom, it is principle, it is the entry of insight into compassion, it is reverence, it is yielding, it is righteousness, it is reason, it is the mind of Avalokiteśvara, it is the very mind of the Buddha.

One attains the great profound mind; regarding the characteristics of that mind, there is no coarseness and no agitation, no distraction and no confusion, no abruptness and no violence, no darkness and no delusion. It is patience, it is concentration, it is wisdom, it is awakening. It is...
This is discernment; this is clarity, this is examination; this is caution, this is deliberation. This is the mind of Mañjuśrī. To enter it is to enter the Buddha-mind.

Having given rise to the aspirational mind, regarding its mental characteristics, one is without weariness or fatigue, without indolence or rest, without retreat or turning back, without negligence or dissipation.
This is progress, this is method; this is aspiration, this is power; this is courage, this is ferocity; this is vitality, this is arousal. This is...
This is the realization of the ultimate; this is the mind of Samantabhadra; this is the very mind of the Buddha. These three minds constitute the true practice of the Bodhisattva.

When each and every thought is perfected, one immediately attains the Great Way without depending on rebirth in another realm. Practicing the myriad virtues directly, the Bodhisattva is able to understand the Buddha’s intentions and hear the Buddha’s teachings.
For the sake of rebirth, they cultivate the practices for rebirth; upon hearing these teachings, they simply invoke the name of the Buddha.
Those who have cultivated merit are all born by way of the womb, either within a celestial palace or within a lotus flower.
For five hundred years and twelve kalpas, they do not see the body of the Buddha nor hear the True Dharma.

However, if there are those who awaken to the five great wisdoms, they immediately attain birth by transformation upon a precious throne, surrounded by the great bodhisattvas of Amitābha Buddha. Immediately—
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, they immediately heard the True Dharma and immediately gave rise to faith. They swiftly attained understanding of the five wisdoms:
namely, the Buddha-wisdom, which is the fundamental, perfect penetration of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings; the Great Wisdom of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Dharma-realm;
the Inconceivable Wisdom of Entry, which is the inconceivable liberation in which Bodhisattvas abide; and the Great Expedient Means of Sovereign Mastery of [the name of] the Bodhisattva.
The Great Wisdom that cannot be described by the intellect; the wondrous emptiness of true emptiness; the peerless, impartial, and supreme wisdom of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Prajñā;
the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas; and the One Vehicle Great Wisdom of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas who practice for rebirth in that land desire to attain birth through transformation; therefore, they cultivate the five wisdoms.

Amitābha Buddha, through the power of his original vows, bestows grace and awakens them. By means of these five wisdoms, they realize the unsurpassed Great Way of all Buddhas without depending on rebirth.
Those of the four classes who practice the myriad virtues directly in this way are called those with superior karmic conditions who obtain benefit in this very life.
What constitutes a person of inferior capacity who gains benefit in a future life?

It refers to those bodhisattvas of dull faculties and ignorance who, although they see such skillful means of the Buddhas, do not understand or awaken to them, and do not resolve upon the path of the great practice of a bodhisattva, but instead fixate their thoughts only on the happiness and long life of that buddha-land;
such are these foolish people. Or there may be bodhisattvas who merely recite the name.
Constantly and single-mindedly recollect the Buddha of Infinite Life with an undistracted mind, entering only this path. Do not perceive the right or wrong, good or bad of others;
do not contemplate the superiority or inferiority, the high or low of other teachings; do not dwell upon the conduct of others, nor respond to their praise or blame, or their trust or suspicion.
Do not turn toward or away from, nor distance yourself from or approach the teachings of others. Fearing only one’s own transgressions and evils, one should solely repent for oneself.
Having already dispelled distraction and agitation, one merely reproaches oneself for lacking the Way and the Dharma; one merely feels shame for oneself being improper and disharmonious.
By cultivating single-mindedness, one naturally achieves goodness and forgets desire, as well as forgetting wrong views and wrong knowledge.
Being without fault or transgression, one naturally brings forth a heart of filial piety, compassion, kindness, gentleness, uprightness, and peace. Life—
When the time of death arrives, they remain far removed from all grasping and attachment, thereby transcending birth and death.
They are reborn within the womb of a lotus flower in the lower grade of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, free from suffering and affliction, dwelling in peace, bliss, and joy.

After the passage of some kalpas, the lotus flower opens, whereupon they behold the unsurpassed marks and signs of that Buddha and hear that Buddha preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle, gradually opening toward the holy.

Awakening. Next, one attains the state of a sage (*ārya*). However, there may be bodhisattvas who are stubbornly desirous and malevolent, constantly committing acts of killing, being deeply attached to the taste of meat, stealing the wealth of others, and seeking great riches, fortune, clothing, and palaces. They engage in sexual misconduct with beautiful women, suffer from grief and sorrow, and have short lifespans.

Yet they forcefully seek long life; their desires are without limit or end, and they do not understand the principles of the world. With darkened minds and deluded views, they fall below the level of the sages.
Instruction: Even when sages demonstrate their transformative teachings, they do not speak thus to such foolish people.

According to that person’s nature and disposition, when they hear described the wondrous matters of the World of Ultimate Bliss—adorned with a hundred jewels, filled with precious gems, where food and drink of a hundred flavors abound, and where nectar gushes forth so that one may travel with sovereign ease according to every wish—and even that the lifespan of the Bodhisattvas and sentient beings therein is [immeasurable]...

For immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it is beyond the reach of seers and immortals. Its human marks and signs are wondrous and beautiful; its celestial maidens are peerless. Joy and bliss are inexhaustible.
There is no distinction of day or night, nor the coming of spring, summer, autumn, or winter. There is neither cold nor heat; it is like the years of a celestial palace.

Yet even within that palace, it stands preeminent and without rival. It transcends the path of speech and is extinguished of all mental activity. It causes all foolish people to desire what they long for.
Having attained their aspiration for rebirth, they gradually advance toward the realm of the Buddha. Delighting in the reforming of evil conduct, they harmonize well with the Noble Path.

Remaining far removed from false poisons, they enjoy peace and happiness in the present life. At the end of their lives, according to their wishes, they immediately proceed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Born within the womb of a lotus flower, when the time comes for it to open, they behold the signs of the Pure Land. This state surpasses all human realms, celestial palaces, and heavenly paradises; thus, their aspirations are fulfilled.
Sufficient. By practicing the bodhisattva path, one ultimately attains enlightenment. These two classes of people are called those who, having been born later, possess inferior capacities.

Such are the characteristics of these two types who obtain benefit; because they receive great benefit, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas pass away from this world to be reborn in other Buddha-lands, except for those who, due to their own ignorance and lack of wisdom, do not know the principles and possess a darkened mind.

Yet they forget to understand the meaning and principles of the holy teachings; considering themselves superior and others inferior, they instruct others according to their own private intellect, desiring to be companions for their own ignorance, and taking these inferior practices to be supreme. As for how to eliminate such [practices] regarding the most excellent and superior conduct:
this is the slandering of the True Dharma, for it turns one's back upon the original vow of that Tathāgata. How does it turn its back upon that original vow?

It is the mind. That Amitābha Buddha constantly teaches the One Vehicle and constantly contemplates the One Vehicle, desiring only that all sentient beings of the lower direction awaken to the wondrous path of the One Vehicle; it is not his fundamental intent to employ inferior practices.
He enters the state of guarding the constant and protects the practice of the Great Way in the Sahā world; he does not take dwelling in peace in Sukhāvatī as his practice.

The original intent was simply to inspire a great vow so that one might attain rebirth with single-minded devotion. It is because foolish people are unable to achieve success through such practice that they must not stop;
rather, they should establish the vow for rebirth. In the Buddha’s mind, there is no distinction between the thought of the Sahā world and the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
The Sahā world and the Land of Peaceful Nurturing are universally equal; this realm and other realms differ in no way whatsoever. That...
The Buddha’s mind is without interval; in every thought-moment, he attends to the minds of others. Why is this?
Because you, one Buddha, and all Buddhas are of one essence within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). There is no distinction between this Buddha and other Buddhas.

Even a great sovereign among men has no sense of self, yet when attending to himself and others, his mind makes no distinction; how much more so for a Tathāgata who has perfected the fruits [of the path], such as Brahmā, the King of Gods?
The retribution is even more pure; throughout the heavens above and the earth below, no difference is seen with the eye, let alone regarding the Tathāgata of the Stage of Perfected Fruition.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, previously you spoke of the light that universally illumines sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
What does this mean? The Buddha said: "Ānanda, this illumination by light is not characterized by the thought 'I am mindful' or 'mindfulness of me.'"
The distinction between them is as follows: the realm of illumination is the *sattvāloka-buddha-samādhi*.

When this samādhi is perfected, one sees that "this mind is the Buddha" and understands the principle of the *dharmakāya*, thereby penetrating the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The radiance of the *dharmakāya* constantly illuminates the ten directions;

there is nothing further to be illuminated. That which illuminates is the distinction. When one's own mind merges with that radiance, one naturally abides within this light; therein, there is only [the light].
That Buddha’s original vow while on the bodhisattva path was to take them in and not abandon them.

He addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva accomplishes the ten recollections of the Buddha, the three minds, and the five wisdoms, how is that dharma perfected? First, such a bodhisattva shall remain forever in this land;
it is certain that they cannot seek rebirth in a pure land. The Buddha said, “Ānanda, if a bodhisattva lives in a world where no Buddha resides...”

Regarding the realms: those who yearn for the Tathāgata, desiring to be born in a pure land in another direction to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and experience the joy of the Dharma—meaning those who achieve even one [of the practices] within the Dharma—shall immediately attain rebirth in a pure land in another direction.

Furthermore, those who are born in the Tuṣita Heaven shall immediately attain rebirth in the highest grade of the highest birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where they shall at that time behold the Honored One, Amitābha.
The Buddhas, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the Bodhisattvas shall immediately travel to see all the Buddhas;
they shall hear the True Dharma, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and all Mahāyāna teachings.
Those who dwell in the capital city shall also attain rebirth in the forty-nine-tiered palaces of mani-jewels, where they shall directly behold me, Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, and...

He saw the Medicine Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-rāja and others; he immediately saw making offerings to the Teacher, Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī, Kṣitigarbha, Vimalakīrti, and Ākāśagarbha, as well as other bodhisattvas difficult to behold.

He also saw making offerings to Acala, the Yakṣa of Majestic Virtue, and the Trailokyavijaya Vidyārāja, who is difficult to behold even in three lifetimes. He likewise saw making offerings to [the deity] Prajñāntaka.
Cai-jixiang (Talent-Auspiciousness), the Bodhisattva Mahādeva King of Much Learning, and others likewise immediately beheld Mākāśyapa, Śāriputra, and the other bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
They then heard of the Great Vehicle, the Dharma for attaining Buddhahood. They addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when entering the city of Ānandapura, what constitutes the difficulty regarding the attainment of peaceful rebirth in that land? The Buddha said: "Ānanda, it is the city of the Ānandapura devas."
This palace is a realm of outflows (*sāsrava*). All ordinary beings who practice the ten wholesome deeds, while mindful of Maitreya, shall immediately attain rebirth there.
It is likewise for all who are mindful of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, or Mañjuśrī.
The Buddhas constantly abide within this palace; all ordinary beings always behold the Buddhas. This land is that of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because the Buddha has perfected his buddha-field, the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is a land of pure lapis lazuli.
Within this palace, it is as if Vimalakīrti had severed off the land of Abhirati in the eastern direction and brought it into his room;

while the Tathāgata Akṣobhya remained within that room, because he had severed and taken it there, when the assembly concluded, that land returned to its original place. This palace is precisely that perfected buddha-field.

Therefore, the three periods of time are eternally abiding, and there is no returning to one's original place. Based on this principle, it is generally easy for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to attain rebirth there.
Since the world of Sukhāvatī is a realm of outflow-free purity (*anāsrava-kṣetra*), even those who have exhausted their taints (*kṣīṇāsrava*)—the bhikṣus—may not yet go there.

Why is this so? Although they have exhausted the taints, these are merely minor fetters (*parītta-saṃyojana*); they still proceed by way of the path of taints. That Land of Peace and Bliss is a Mahāyāna realm. For this reason...
This is difficult. There is only rebirth there. Regarding all ordinary beings who rely on the two types of birth: what are these two births?
It is because of the power of that Amitābha Buddha’s original vow and through the efficacy of skillful means that he creates lotus flowers, which are divided into nine grades.
Within these flowers, there is "womb-birth" (*garbhaja*); the highest grade takes one night, while the lowest grade lasts for twelve great kalpas. As it says in the Sūtra...
Depending on the magnitude of one's merit or the gravity of one's karmic obstructions, the opening of the lotus flower varies in its speed—some being slow and others fast.
This refers to what are known as the "two births. As for the first birth: upon the end of the present life, one is reborn from this land.

Within a lotus flower—though this lotus flower exists in that land, that which is within the lotus flower is not of that land—it naturally accords with the Great Way of all Buddhas after the passage of many kalpas.
One repents of former transgressions, and once the transgressions have been extinguished, [one attains realization].
They naturally attain awakening and practice the Great Way; this constitutes one lifetime. When they practice the Great Way, the lotus flower immediately opens.
At that time, they are truly born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, where Amitābha Buddha and the great Bodhisattvas dwell, surrounded by them.
This is truly rebirth. Regarding these two types of rebirth, there are also nine grades. Furthermore, there is one type of external rebirth, which consists of four classes:
First, those who practice the six perfections, awaken to enlightenment, and develop wisdom; such bodhisattvas immediately attain direct rebirth before Amitābha Buddha.
Second, great arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) who suddenly turn their minds and resolve to cultivate the Mahāyāna path; they too [attain rebirth].

That path leads directly to birth before Amitābha Buddha. Third, although one has not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and has not yet attained the six *pāramitās*, by upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the scripture of the Single Buddha Vehicle—and practicing according to its teachings, one will, according to one’s capacity, attain access to the Buddha’s wisdom and vision, and through opening, showing, awakening, and entering [into that state], one shall directly attain birth before Amitābha Buddha. Fourth.

Those who receive and uphold this unsurpassed divine mantra—the single, collective dhāraṇī of the divine and expedient arts of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amoghasiddhi, Amitābha Buddha, and all Buddhas of the three periods of time; the various secret divine mantras and the secret mantras of all Buddhas—will have their incantations successfully accomplished.
Therefore, it is able to be achieved; it is not that the Buddhas provide private assistance or achieve it for them privately. It is...

The mantra-rites are accomplished. Evil is transformed by the mantra into goodness; delusion is transformed by the mantra into awakening; sin is transformed by the mantra into merit; the ordinary is transformed by the mantra into the holy;
obstructions are transformed by the mantra into purity; and difficulty is transformed by the mantra into ease. Regarding the power of the mantra, it is a power that surpasses all Buddhas.

One should visualize the five Buddhas seated within the full moon disk of one’s mental focus, with Vairocana Tathāgata in the center emitting yellow light, Akṣobhya emitting blue light, and Ratna... [emitting yellow light].
A red light arises; Amitābha is white light; Amoghapāśa is purple light. With the right hand, one can form the seal of five-colored light.
Reciting the divine mantra, the *Prabhāsa-dhāraṇī*, whether for oneself or for others, one immediately realizes the Dharmakāya and attains direct rebirth before Amitābha Buddha.
This mantra for rebirth makes no distinction between good people and evil people, or the wise and the foolish.
The power of the Buddha does not reach them; it is only through the power of the mantra that success is achieved. However, there is one obstacle from past lives:

those who have not formed a karmic connection, those who have not planted the seeds of cause, and those who have not encountered this mantra. Even if they do encounter the mantra, if they do not give rise to faith, they will lose a great benefit.
Regarding such evil persons, what would the five Buddhas and all the Buddhas say? [The interlocutor] addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are..."
"Evil persons, hearing that this power of the mantra possesses such merit, might still commit evil deeds because of that very power of the mantra. What do you think?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, it is as you have said. Because of its principle, the Buddhas keep this secret and do not bestow it upon people indiscriminately.
Only those with past roots of goodness encounter this mantra. Nevertheless, even so, one who maintains the mantra with faith and relies upon the Three [Refuges]..."

Through the power of the Secret [Dharma], one naturally forgets evil and naturally casts off transgressions; with body and mind purified, one becomes a person of goodness. He addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, regarding what was previously taught—that ten recitations lead to birth in the lowest grade of the lower level—yet now you speak of being transformed by these ten recitations to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, how is this to be understood?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What was previously taught refers to the time when, at the end of life, one relies upon..."
The Teaching on Knowledge: One who possesses the ten recitations but daily commits evil and rebellious acts has little merit at that time;

therefore, they are reborn in the lowest grade of the lower birth. As for those spoken of now, they are the practitioners who constantly cultivate the ten recitations until they reach the path of the ten recitations;
therefore, they are reborn upon the precious throne. They address the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as stated in the Original Vow of Amitābha..."

"Except for those born with the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and those who have slandered the Dharma. As for those of the lowest grade of birth, even those who have slandered the Dharma or committed the five heinous crimes can all attain rebirth.
Why, then, is there such a distinction? The Buddha said, "Ānanda, it is as stated in their original vows:
'Because these are all Buddhas who have perfected the method for attaining rebirth, [the offenses] are excluded. If that Tathāgata, out of mindfulness for my Buddha-nature..."
It is unreasonable that an evil person who has committed the grave offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) should attain rebirth there.

If such were the case, Amitābha Buddha would not have fulfilled his vows, nor would he have perfected the path to Buddhahood; he would instead fall into the fault of irrationality and would not be a Great Sage.
As for those people of the lowest grade and lowest birth, by relying on the teachings of wisdom and consciousness, they sincerely repent their former evils and former offenses.
Abandoning all evil and transforming their minds to become pure, they immediately achieve a correct mind. Endowed with the ten recitations, they become newly transformed persons.
It should be known that such a person possesses a correct mind and is without fault; they are among the ranks of virtuous people and will naturally attain rebirth there.
This is not due to any partiality on the part of that Buddha, nor is it solely through the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment. Such a person is indeed one of the virtuous;

why would that Buddha not empower them? Regardless of whether one is an ordinary person or a sage, concerning birth in a single lifetime—specifically, being born as a virtuous person—one is thereby made a leader of all.
It is easy to reach the celestial palaces, but difficult to attain An-yang (Sukhāvatī). This also concerns ordinary beings and sages regarding two types of birth:
namely, for an evil person, it is easy to be born in the world of An-yang, whereas it is difficult to reach the Universal Sovereign (Dharmākara).

However, for those who rely on mantras, practice the three mysteries (triguhyas), and walk the path of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, both An-yang and the Universal Sovereign are equally easy to attain; there is no longer any difficulty.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the mantras and mudrās of the three secret practices, ordinary people of inferior and foolish capacity are able to cultivate them.
However, as for the moon in the heart, they are unable to do so. How should they practice? The Buddha said:
"Ānanda, practitioners of mantras have four types of faculties. There are three types of practitioners with superior wisdom."
The Bhagavān was dwelling on Mount Laṅkā, teaching the supreme Mahāyāna Dharma to a great assembly of Bodhisattvas, including Mahāmati and various celestial beings.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "If you and others among the humans and devas truly desire to attain Buddhahood, you should directly cultivate the Tathāgata’s true dhyāna.
Discipline the body, discipline the speech, and discipline the mind; for it is through such discipline that those who are distracted can enter the noble wisdom of self-realization."
Regarding the realm: one accomplishes the unsurpassed Buddha-body. Ānanda, you should know that this dhyāna accomplishes its essence through three kinds of meanings.
First, by means of the methods of practice, the characteristics of phenomena, and the principles of the Dharma, one eliminates erroneous principles and realizes the correct principle.
Second, one embraces the Noble Path; with a rectified mind, one treats and subdues the distracted mind, realizing the mind of the Path.
Third, one attains the realization of the Path through the awakening of samādhi, transforming the ordinary nature and manifesting the fruit of sainthood. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This Tathāgata-dhyāna consists of preliminary dhyāna, the dhyāna of attaining the Path within [the middle], and the ultimate true dhyāna. What is the dhyāna of skillful means? One should contemplate the *vīpaśyanā*..."
The Vairocana Buddha is the single path of the principle of emptiness, the Dharma-body of this Tathāgata Vairocana.
The nature of phenomena is the body of the Dharma-realm, whose essence is empty space, pervading all realms. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If you first wish to contemplate the Tathāgata’s essence of empty space, you should first contemplate and realize the essence of your own entire mind—formless, utterly detached, quiescent, and void."
There is not even a single hair [of self]. That which I (my possession) am is this void Dharma-body.

By contemplating it until the mind is realized as the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of absolute emptiness, one attains the state where all things are an unmoving realm; this is the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

One who is able to enter this completely becomes free from all afflictions and will never again return to birth and death. This is called the "preparatory skillful means of dhyāna" and is also called the "initial stage of the Mahāyāna."
Entering the gate to contemplate the Way, the Buddha told Ānanda: "What is the dhyāna of attaining the Way within?
When a Bodhisattva wishes to contemplate the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm body, they should contemplate the single mark of their own mind.

This primordial wondrous principle is perfectly full, containing oceans of subtle atoms, and is itself the essence of self-arisen and self-awakened noble wisdom, possessing the virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. These are the five virtues of a Bodhisattva."
One should practice this path of Tathāgata-dhyāna. What are the five virtues of a bodhisattva?

Reflecting now upon the past, incalculable great kalpas ago—beyond immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) immeasurables of kalpas, and beyond immeasurable immeasurables of kalpas prior to those—the Buddhas known as Immeasurable-Immeasurable (*amitāmita*) appeared in the world, as well as [those] immeasurable immeasurables [of others].
Among all Buddhas, there is one Vairocana Buddha. This Vairocana Buddha, by means of a single body, differentiates his wisdom-body and meditative-concentration-body to become two bodhisattvas.
The first is the Wisdom-body Bodhisattva, named Ghoṣa-pratibhāsa (Responsive Sound);
he is the right side of this Vairocana Buddha’s body. The second is the Meditative-Concentration-body Bodhisattva.
Their names are Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who is the left portion of the body of Vairocana Buddha; and Guṇasvara Bodhisattva.

Based upon the fundamental substance of wisdom, the three aspects of principle, wisdom, and compassion are differentiated to form three bodhisattvas. This is the original body of the principle-dharma.
The right hand, representing wisdom, is the Bodhisattva Ārya-Śabdaguṇarāja; the left hand, representing compassion, is the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, based upon the fundamental essence of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), differentiates into two bodies: wisdom and practice.
They become two Bodhisattvas: the fundamental body is the practice and vow [of Samantabhadra], while the distinct body of knowledge and vision is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
The responsive Bodhisattvas abide in practice, dwelling, and vows. The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who presides over the East from the West, abides in compassion.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, who presides over the West from the East, abides in wisdom. The [Bodhisattva] of the South... abides in conduct.
The Northern direction presides over ritual activity (*karma*). Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva abides in ritual activity. The Northern direction presides over the wisdom of the Southern direction.

Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva abides in sincerity and faith. The Center presides over the virtuous functions of the four directions. Therefore, these are the bodhisattvas with whom this Sahā world has a karmic affinity.
Since the essential bodies of the dharma-nature (*dharmakāya*) of these five bodhisattvas pervade the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). And...
The sentient beings of the human and celestial realms possess five kinds of rational mind. What are these five kinds of rational mind?
First, a Bodhisattva of the Śākya lineage should contemplate their own primordial mind. Therein lies a single mind of great kindness and great compassion;

this is the mind of all Buddhas, the mind of all devas, and the virtuous person in the world. Such a person is born in accordance with the harmony of heaven and earth, and is able to bring benefit to the human world.
In this world, it is for the sake of such people that compassion arises; this is the natural principle by which the mind is endowed with its essence.

By binding various states of mind, one forms a heart of loving harmony; by binding various karmas, one forms the karma of nurturing. This mind and these karmas constitute a purely wholesome mind and purely wholesome karma.
As for those who are evil people in the world, they are individuals born in opposition to Heaven and Earth; they encounter calamities, misfortunes, suffering, and harm because of this.
The human mind possesses compassion; this is the mind endowed with its natural rationality. When all mental states are integrated, they form a heart of empathy and pity;
when all karmic actions are integrated, they form the karma of rescue and relief. This mind and these actions constitute pure goodness—both pure wholesome mind and pure wholesome karma.
Toward one’s parents it becomes filial piety; toward one’s children and servants it becomes wisdom. This mind is the supreme, most excellent mind; it is the nature of Heaven.
It covers and nurtures all things; by being able to refine and mature this mind, one attains the state that is eternal and unchanging.

This is the second *āśaya-ratna-citta* (jewel-mind of intention) that is definitively accomplished. A bodhisattva should contemplate their own mental nature and possess a single mind of firm principle;
this constitutes the practice of a bodhisattva, the path of the celestial hosts, and that upon which all worlds depend.
When the principle is correct, one stands firm; when one relies on the Way and its Principle, one attains benefit.

This mind is the mind of the Way, and this principle is the principle of the Way. Good people rely upon it and thereby attain benefit; it is not that the mind of principle possesses a "benefiting mind," for the Way and its Principle inherently provide benefit.
When evil people act, they are overcome; it is not that the mind of principle possesses a "conquering mind," for the Way and its Principle inherently bring about conquest. This is the mind.
Toward the sovereign, one achieves loyalty; toward the multitude of fellow beings, one achieves propriety. This mind is the very substance of Heaven, which must be maintained with steadfastness.
If one can cultivate this mind to maturity, one will attain a state that is eternal and immutable; this is what is called the definitive accomplishment of the *triśakya* (triple-great) rational mind.
A bodhisattva should observe their own mental nature and find within it a single mind characterized by reverent decorum and ritual propriety. This is...
The Dharma of the High Heaven is the Dharma of all the Sages. Its essence is eternal and unchanging; its function responds to the times.
Great Brahmā King establishes this Dharma in the heavens; the Golden Wheel-turning Sage King establishes this Dharma on earth;
the Buddhas establish this Dharma in the Dharma-realm; and Bodhisattvas establish this Dharma among humans. This mind is the true mind; this Dharma is the true Dharma.
The Dharma: this mind is able to establish the methods of the world and the positions of honor and subordination, as well as high and low, within heaven and earth.
When it is able to mature through conditions, this mind achieves a state that is permanent, eternal, and unchanging; this is called the mind of the essential nature of the four types of *prajñā*.
A bodhisattva should observe their own mind. There is a single wisdom that illuminates the mind; this is the light of all Buddhas and the light of all devas.
If there were no light in the world—with its mountains, plains, valleys, rivers, seas, bridges, and boats—how could one travel anywhere?
Among humans, there are matters of right and wrong, and the myriad phenomena of delusion and awakening; without the examination of wisdom, how could one discern them?

It is said: Whether great or small, all are entrusted with wisdom. To be able to refine and master this mind so as to achieve a state that is eternal and unchanging—this constitutes the definitive accomplishment of the five *tathatā* (thusness) natures of the rational mind. A Bodhisattva should contemplate the principle of their own mind;
therein lies the single heart of the source of the sincere Way, which is the virtue and path of the *sattva*. By relying on this, one emerges from the mundane world.
World, if one loses this sincerity and faith, then all phenomena will have no basis for attainment. The aforementioned four minds all attain this stage as their position;
by being able to refine and master these minds, one achieves the state of permanence and immutability. This is called "definitive accomplishment."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What is called the rational mind of Śākyamuni takes great wisdom and great indulgence as its function.
Furthermore, there is the rational mind of Āśi which restrains it; yet it does not save [the former], allowing the rational mind of Śākyamuni to indulge in wisdom and indulge in indulgence."
The *āśraya-ratna-citta* (the mind of rationality based on reliance) takes the accomplishment or failure of further [actions] as its task.

Furthermore, it is restrained by the *prajñā-ratna-citta* (the mind of rationality based on wisdom), which does not permit the *āśraya-ratna-citta* to act with unrestrained success or unrestrained failure. The *prajñā-ratna-citta* takes extensive calculation and far-reaching discernment as its task.
Furthermore, it is restrained by the *śīla-ratna-citta* (the mind of rationality based on ethical discipline), which does not permit the *prajñā-ratna-citta*...
The rational mind (*dharmatā-citta*) reckons according to its own will. Śakra, the rational mind, takes exclusive yielding and exclusive restraint as its business.
Furthermore, the *tunmei* (dhyāna-meditation) rational mind restrains it, yet does not pardon it;

thus it causes Śakra’s rational mind to yield at will and restrain at will, while the *tunmei* rational mind takes partial reality and sole conformity as its business. Furthermore, the Śākya rational mind restrains it.

Thus, while not pardoning the fact that Tan’s mind has not yet attained its fundamental nature, his outward appearance is indeed identical [to the enlightened state]. In this way, there is a principle of mutual regulation and interrogation;
yet, one does not pardon even a hair-tip of delusion. The Buddha told Ānanda: "The five fundamental natures and minds attain mutual regulation when they abide in their original positions.
They harmonize with the fundamental principle without confusion, just like the moat of a Wheel-Turning Sage King's city."
Stone upon stone is layered and mutually constrained; they are mutually checked so as not to scatter or fall, and thus the structure of the city possesses the virtue of firmness.
The five natures and the rational mind likewise constrain and check one another, ensuring that neither excess nor deficiency occurs.
Thus, Śākyamuni abides in goodness, Āśī resides in suitability, Prajñā abides in principle, Śikṣā abides in truth, and Dharmatā...
They ultimately abide in the Way, yet each occupies its own station. The world entirely relies upon them; they establish the great security. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These five natures and the rational mind are but a single mind. They are both shared and unshared;

it is precisely because they exist that they achieve their fulfillment, and it is precisely because they are absent that one attains their excellence. It is like a ring without end; one must be able to contemplate its fundamental substance."
It becomes firm and is further realized through its application. This clearly demonstrates that by employing immeasurable phenomena and affairs, one brings all things to a state of goodness.
Thus, for those who have accomplished the five natures of the rational mind: those of the lower grade reside among humans;

they cultivate the path of the sages and saints to benefit themselves and others, bringing peace and happiness to the world, and leading sentient beings into the Bodhisattva path. Those of the middle grade enter [the path].
Celestial Immortals (*deva-rṣi*). They cultivate the bodhisattva path, transforming dragons, ghosts, spirits, and enchantresses to lead them toward the Buddha-way and protect the world.

Those of the superior grade are reborn in celestial palaces, where they cultivate the bodhisattva path, protecting heaven and stabilizing earth to benefit sentient beings and all things. The most superior grade is indeterminate:
they may interact with those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; or they may dwell among humans, as celestial immortals, or in celestial palaces. Or they may dwell...
In the pure lands of the Buddhas in other directions, they manifest infinite emanations and countless forms to practice the Buddha-way, benefiting themselves and others.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If even such a virtuous mind as this can still be constrained and suppressed, so that it becomes a truly wholesome state, how much more so for an evil mind?
All evil minds are fundamentally the nature of the five consciousnesses; when they are constrained and suppressed, they cannot arise. The Buddha—
I say to Ānanda: When an evil mind arises, there are two sources of such evil deeds. The first is called the source of exceeding goodness;
the second is called the source of emptiness. What is the source of exceeding goodness? It is when the five natures of the rational mind are biased toward one and do not remain as five together.

Furthermore, each one individually exceeds its limit. When those who do not maintain the fivefold balance offer reproof and interrogation, then the rational nature of their Buddha-nature becomes [obstructed].
