The delusive vapor of ignorance then floods and invades them; through the fault of such delusion, they quickly give rise to an evil mind.

That which was compassion becomes a mind of attachment; that which was righteousness becomes a mind of hatred and harm; that which was wisdom becomes a mind of flattery and deceit; that which was reverent decorum becomes a mind of sycophancy;
and that which was sincerity and trustworthiness becomes a mind of partiality. This greatly damages the Noble Path. It is, for example, like this:
When treating a patient and taking medicine to cure an illness, one may take it in excess, whereby the medicine returns as a toxic poison. How can this be called a source of emptiness?

If one employs the rational mind according to the five natures but does not attain constant perfection, yet suddenly lets it go, then within that interval, false thoughts such as greed, stinginess, anger, hatred, delusion, and confusion will immediately arise. If such a mind arises, then this mind will quickly become established.
One incurs remorse as one’s body commits the evil deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and fraudulent conduct;

and one’s speech produces the evil words of harshness, slander, lying, and frivolous chatter, thereby destroying others, damaging one’s own person, bringing shame upon one’s reputation, and causing the loss of one’s descendants.

This extinguishes the lineage of delusion. Those who die and fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras will never escape the cycle of birth and death, nor its sorrows, lamentations, suffering, and afflictions.

O Worldly Ones, it is like those with the six supernormal powers among world-transcending śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or those with the five supernormal powers among worldly devas, immortals, spirits, and ghosts;
if they were to see a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of their hand, they would perceive its full form from beginning to end. Thus it is.
It cannot be explained exhaustively. Thus, by observing all the atoms of the world, one attains freedom from all delusions and the fulfillment of all virtues;

this stage is called the "Accomplished Samādhi. This is termed the "Middle Attainment of the Path Dhyāna," and is also called the "Great Vehicle’s Middle-of-the-Middle Constant Practice of Path-Observation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What is the subsequent 'Ultimate Reality Dhyāna'? It is when a Bodhisattva wishes to observe the entire body of the Tathāgata."

Regarding the attainment of the Buddha-body: by means of the mind of Śākyamuni as the Bodhisattva Responding to Sound, one cultivates wisdom and dhyāna, becomes detached from the mark of a self (jīva), and attains bliss.
Exhausting the afflictions of the mind, intellect, and consciousness within the conditioned, one reaches the fruit of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and realizes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.
Abiding in无缘 (unconditioned) compassion, one cultivates noble dhyāna with the *āśaya* (resolute intention) of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

Free from the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*), one attains the constant virtue (*nitya-guṇa*) and exhausts the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) of the ālayavijñāna. Reaching the secret fruit of Buddhahood of Akṣobhya, one realizes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Abiding in the vow of non-action, one cultivates self-meditation through the prajñā-mind of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Free from the mark of self, one attains the virtue of self and exhausts all that pertains to "I" and "mine," reaching the fruit of Buddhahood where the flowers bloom.

One realizes the Wisdom of Equality and abides in merit that is unobtainable. Through the śīla-mind of the Bodhisattva Śrī, one cultivates awakening-meditation. Free from the marks of persons, one attains purity.

Virtue. Exhausting the five faculties and the great consciousness of conditioned phenomena, one reaches the Buddha-fruit of the Celestial Drum Sound and realizes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done.
Abiding in non-conceptual knowledge and vision, one cultivates the Tathāgata-dhyāna with the mind of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, free from views of both phenomena and their negation.
Having attained *pāramitā*, exhausted the delusions of ignorance and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and reached the fruit of Buddhahood as the Great Muni,

he realized the wisdom that takes the essence of the *dharmadhātu* as its object and dwells in the fruit of untainted awakening (*anāsrava-bodhi*). All Buddhas of the three times rely upon this path to transform causes into fruits,
attaining the name of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, and Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām.

The Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—this is called the ultimate true dhyāna. It is also called the Great Vehicle’s Final Abode of Attaining the Way through Contemplation.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Regarding those who practice this dhyāna that brings about Buddhahood, those of inferior capacity attain perfect enlightenment at the very moment they first resolve their minds;
while remaining on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they immediately awaken to Buddhahood. Those of middling capacity..."
These constitute the three stages. Entering the path of Samantabhadra, those of the superior grade of practice are called "those who will attain Buddhahood in one lifetime" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Those of the most superior grade of practice are none other than the Buddhas of the three periods of time. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Those who cultivate this Tathāgata-dhyāna, although they have not yet attained actual practice or actual realization during the initial, middle, or final stages, for those in the world, it is the mundane path that treats the human realm; it is the path of the inferior grade."
Those who attain the stage of a virtuous person; those with the middling path attain the stage of a worthy person; those with the superior path attain the stage of a sage.
Those of present brilliance will be reborn in celestial palaces after death. As for those who transcend the world, they cultivate the path of a śramaṇa. Those with the inferior path...
Those who attain the stage of a virtuous person; those of middling capacity on the path attain the stage of awakening; and those of superior capacity on the path attain the stage of samādhi.

They experience wondrous and extraordinary benefits in the present life and will be reborn in a pure land in future lives. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, celestial beings, spirits, and all the people were filled with great joy.
